To evaluate high-gaussian beam slicing in laser-wakefield accelerators, an experimental setup was developed that uses a single-stage system to produce intense photon flash at X-ray energies. A 20 micrometer titanium foil was utilized to scatter wakefield-driven radiation in the laboratory frame of reference, achieving a peak dose of 10^5 Gy. This dose level is sufficient for radiography of electron beam profiles, thus enabling profile monitoring of laser-wakefield-driven electron beams.

In the context of the CP-even lightest Higgs boson $h$ and the CP-odd heavy Higgs boson $A$, which are part of the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model type-II, we analyzed the impact of squark loop contributions on the light Higgs boson $h$ decaying into two photons, which was initially analyzed by Degrassi et al. We then used the results to establish connections between the experimental data from the LHC and two key parameters: the soft breaking Z2 potential parameter $\phi_S$ and the CP-violating Z2 breaking parameter $\phi_A$. We found that the $\phi_S$ value is largely dependent on the $\tan\beta$ value and is more pronounced when $\tan\beta$ values are more moderate. We also discovered that the $\phi_A$ value is more dependent on the masses of the Higgs bosons $M_B$ and $M_C$, which in turn affects the impact on the other two fermions. We found that the $\phi_A$ value is more significant for bottom and tauon quarks than it is for top quarks. We then used the experimental data from the LHC to establish limits on the $\phi_S$ and $\phi_A$ values and found that limits on the $\phi_S$ value are more significant for moderate $\tan\beta$ values and bottom quark, whereas limits on the $\phi_A$ value are more significant for large $\tan\

This paper investigates how the value of a universal solution changes in the context of data exchange based on tuple-generating dependencies. A key covered source schema is considered, along with a Kripke structure to analyze how the set of universal solutions evolves as source facts are added one at a time. Our study reveals that the collective universal solutions become consistent and exist only when the data exchange setting has a dependency on a Kripke structure's accessible paths. Our data shows that the collective universal solutions become consistent and exist only when the data exchange setting is fully covered. Our findings also reveal that the collective universal solutions become consistent and exist only when the data exchange setting has a source fact that enables access to all vertices within the Kripke structure. Furthermore, our data highlights scenarios where the collective universal solutions do not exist and remain unchanged, serving as counterexamples to previously established results. Our study builds upon and expands the existing research on data exchange, focusing on first-order data consistency and data existence. Our work also has implications for other areas, such as database repair and integration, by providing insights into how to obtain a desirable universal solution. Our study specifically addresses the question of whether it is possible to obtain a desirable universal solution in the context of data exchange. Our work shows that, under certain conditions, it is indeed possible to obtain a desirable universal solution. Our study also raises the question of whether it is possible to obtain a desirable universal solution in the context of data exchange when the data exchange setting is not fully

pyStoNED is a Python package for implementing various multivariate regression methods that combine 2D image data and a related variable as input, which we also refer to as multivariate regression. We also refer to it as stoNED for Spatiotemporal Noise-ODEmented Regression and provide a flexible tool to perform ODE-based image data analysis and visualisation. The package offers a range of multivariate regression algorithms, including Ridge, Lasso, Elastic-Net, Huber, Quantile, Holt-Daehly Quantile, Holt-Kauss Quantile, and Huber-Kauss Quantile, which we also refer to as QSODR. Furthermore, we provide a simple interface for the Ridge, Lasso, Elastic-Net, Huber, Quantile, and Holt-Daehly Quantile algorithms and offer visualisation options for the results obtained.

This study examines the direct search for neutral scalar particles within a specific two-Higgs doublet model, considering direct gauge interactions and Yukawa couplings involving bottom quarks, and assesses new physics scenarios at the High Luminosity phase of the LHC. The researchers analyze the scenario where heavy charged Higgs particles decay into W bosons and heavier neutral scalars, with the latter reaching an energy level of approximately 800 GeV, and the scalars being produced via gluon fusion and decaying into bottom quark pairs. The study finds that while excluding lighter scalars up to 600 GeV and heavier scalars up to 700 GeV is achievable with moderate Yukawa couplings, it is more challenging for the lightest scalars above 600 GeV and heavier scalars above 700 GeV. Furthermore, it is observed that the search strategy is not impacted by the CP properties of the Yukawa coupling and that the study's results are not significantly affected by background uncertainties.

This study presents the model FPIO, designed to tackle few-shot learning in parsing under the Context-Free Incremental Context-Free Grammar framework. By leveraging FPIO, we can achieve superior performance compared to previous few-shot parsing models even with only 10 annotated training examples. Moreover, FPIO exhibits strong generalization capabilities across various grammars, and it outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in scenarios where as few as 10 training examples are available.

This paper presents a new training strategy for neural-based speech recognition models that builds on existing evidence showing the benefits of diverse training data in speaker and vocabulary diversity. The proposed method employs ensemble-based data augmentation to create multiple versions of a model's parameters, generating a robust model that can effectively handle varied training data and avoid overfitting. The strategy involves a data augmentation process, data sharing, and model ensemble. The data augmentation step randomly adjusts model parameters, mimicking the effects of a larger and more varied training dataset. The data sharing step facilitates the sharing of parameters among multiple data-augmented models. Finally, each model adapts to its unique set of parameters, resulting in an ensemble of varied models. The proposed method has been tested and compared with other state-of-the-art techniques, and it has been shown to outperform them, achieving a 20.4% relative error reduction and outperforming the teacher data augmentation method by 10.4% in a specific dataset setting.

The research paper examines the orbital periods of 11 recently discovered long-period binary Be stars with a focus on their physical properties. These Be stars are categorized into two distinct groups, one comprising stars that have a more normal spectral type, and the other consisting of stars that have a more Be-type spectral classification. Interestingly, the two subgroups are found to have different characteristics, including spectral properties, stellar masses, and orbital periods. Notably, the Be-type group is observed to have shorter orbital periods and more tightly bound systems. Additionally, the researchers conducted a comparative analysis with a collection of 15 other binary Be stars to identify trends and correlations. Ultimately, the study presents a model that explains the evolution of these binary Be systems, including the relationship between orbital periods and mass ratios.

NLP's growing interest in low-resource languages has led to the development of ITN (Indo-Tibetan language name normalization) models using bilingual data. However, the limited public data available hinders the application of ITN. This paper presents a unique data augmentation technique, leveraging a bilingual name dictionary to enhance ITN models. The proposed method outperforms ITN-models trained with the same trilingual data, achieving an improved F1 score of 0.718 versus 0.634. Furthermore, the method can be applied universally to any bilingual pair with a name dictionary, demonstrating its effectiveness across various languages and name datasets.

This paper proves a Faber-Krahn type inequality within a specific subset of Rn, which includes the space Rn itself. The subset is defined by a space called Cn, which consists of convex bodies. We demonstrate that among a family of geometric shapes, the origin-centered hypercubes achieve the minimum first eigenvalue of a particular Hermite operator. The operator is defined by the sum of the squared partial derivatives minus a term involving a specific polynomial, which depends on a point in Rn. The polynomial, Pn, is known as the Zonal polynomial, which allows us to apply our results to a specific type of hypersets, which includes star-shaped sets around the origin, thus extending our results to a broader class of sets.

Deep learning models' behavior is being examined using universal kernels to offer more transparent insights. It's demonstrated that neural tangent kernels outperform traditional kernel methods to provide more interpretable results. A key advantage of neural tangent kernels is their ability to incorporate additional regularization and control hyperparameters, thus limiting model capacity. This flexibility allows for more targeted and transparent modeling. A new regularization technique for linear models is introduced and shown to naturally emerge from neural tangent kernels. It is also shown that neural tangent kernels can incorporate side information and covariates to create more robust models. A new regularization method is proposed to facilitate transparent deep learning, incorporating insights from linear models. It is demonstrated that neural tangent kernels accurately model the behavior of ReLU networks and provide more robust predictions. A new regularization method is proposed to facilitate transparent image classification, using the MNIST dataset. It is shown that neural tangent kernels accurately model the behavior of convolutional neural networks and that a CNN-based model matches empirical results. A new regularization method for graph-structured data is proposed, using node embeddings and an adjacency matrix. It is demonstrated that neural tangent kernels accurately model the behavior of graph neural networks and that a GNN-based model matches empirical results. A new regularization method for transparent deep learning across various machine learning tasks is proposed.

We investigate the behavior of the eigenvalues and wavefunctions in non-Hermitian chains with periodic boundary conditions and focus particularly on correlations of power-laws. Building upon our previous research, which analyzed free fermions on these chains, we now incorporate correlation effects into our study. Specifically, we derive the eigenvalues and wavefunctions for certain types of non-Hermitian chains, such as the extended Hatano-Nelson and Ising models, which exhibit power-law correlations. Our results show that these correlations significantly impact the skin effect and reveal a connection between non-Hermitian physics and critical phenomena.

This research examines the relationship between acoustic characteristics of speech and perceived attributes in female voices produced by neural text-to-speech systems. By analyzing speech from the LibriSpeech female corpus, we found female speech uses acoustic patterns that signal perceived competence, in contrast to male speech which uses less consistent patterns. Through visual and statistical analysis, we found these acoustic patterns consist of a combination of distinct vocal features, with some being more prominent and others contributing subtly. By comparing speech from male and female narrators, we found female speech uses a narrower vocal range, supporting the hypothesis that female voices modulate their acoustic patterns to avoid appearing uncompetent. Overall, our research provides new insights into how female voices balance competence and likability through a gradual modulation of acoustic patterns.

A two-Higgs doublet dark matter model based on a specific $Z_2$ symmetry is proposed, where this symmetry is derived from the requirement that Higgs doublets have distinct parity assignments in different sectors of the model. The stability of the proposed dark matter is ensured by the presence of the $Z_2$ symmetry, and the global $SU(2)_L$ symmetry helps to constrain the potential of the scalar sector. The proposed model is able to explain a variety of dark matter detection results, including direct, indirect, and cosmic ray observations, as well as the baryon asymmetry of the universe.

The influence of the generalized uncertainty principle on quantum mechanics has been examined by modifying the potential in the Schrödinger equation, allowing for the analysis of a model with a general interaction, a harmonic oscillator, and a potential with a $\beta$-deformation, in one, two, and three dimensions. In this work, we apply this model to triaxial nuclei, using it to determine the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions for the prolate and oblate configurations, providing an explanation for the distinct behaviors of energy levels with increasing angular momentum in these shapes.

We establish the existence of feasible quaternary Golay complementary array pairs of length n if n is divisible by 5 to the power of m, where m can be any positive integer. Our research leverages the properties of Golay complementary array pairs and their differences to construct quaternary sequences with Golay complementary pairs, especially focusing on the case where the Golay complementary array pairs have lengths of 2 to the power of r and 4 to the power of s. The feasible Golay complementary array pairs have lengths of n by utilizing recursive methods and computer searches.

The detection of urban 3D scene changes is of significant interest to various fields, including computer vision, robotics, and remote sensing. A key challenge in this field is identifying the most suitable deep learning methods that can operate without labeled data and are resilient to variations in point cloud data. A proposed novel method, the Free-form Point Cloud Change Detection framework, is specifically designed to tackle this issue. The free-form point cloud change detection framework is capable of identifying changes in point clouds without a prior model, using both registered and unregistered point clouds. A key component of this method is a novel feature descriptor that combines multi-scale point features and directional information to effectively describe local changes. A point-wise and global contrastive learning strategy is used to refine feature representations. A novel adaptation of the Hard Negative Mining module is also incorporated to accelerate unsupervised change detection. A benchmark dataset, the Semantic Change Detection Benchmark Dataset, is introduced to rigorously evaluate state-of-the-art change detection techniques. A comprehensive comparison of different deep learning methods, including variations in training and testing datasets, is conducted to establish a baseline for future research. A novel system, the Adaptive Contrastive Learning System, is proposed to automate unsupervised change detection and outperforms state-of-the-art methods, using only unsupervised data. The Free-form Point Cloud Change Detection framework and the SLiCE-3D dataset are publicly available for future research.

Viscosity behavior in a range of related molecular fluids that do not associate can be effectively modeled when using both pressure and density as reference parameters, rather than just pressure at fixed density, rather than using only pressure with an adjusted density exponent. A study involving 48 substances, including noble gases, carbon dioxide, nitrogen, oxygen, and methane, confirmed viscosity scaling across varying temperatures, showing the validity of density-weighted viscosity scaling across related fluids. A comparative analysis of viscosity scaling across related and unrelated fluids, including liquids such as ethanol and toluene, further validated the density-weighted viscosity scaling model's applicability in predicting viscosity behavior.

A novel periodic cosmology model is proposed, encompassing the Big Bang, cosmic inflation, dark energy, and cyclic matter-radiation-Big Bang phases. In this framework, the Lambda-CDM phase is flanked by inflation at its start and by a cyclic matter-radiation-Big Bang period at its end. Each of its components is characterized: cyclic eras feature Matter-CDM with Big-Bang-Nucleosynthesis and Radiation-CDM followed by radiation followed by Big-Bang; inflation is described by quasi-de-Sitter; Lambda-CDM occupies a quasi-de-Sitter state. In this framework, the Big-Bang acts as an interface between two cycles, while the model accounts for cosmic microwave background spectrum and B-mode polarization. Baryon acoustic oscillation, weak gravitational lensing, and supernovae data are also accommodated. Furthermore, B-mode polarization spectrum and cosmic microwave background spectrum can be explained by stochastic gravitational waves originating from prior cosmic events including cyclic matter-radiation-Big Bang periods and prior inflation. B-mode polarization spectrum can also be attributed to gravitational waves resulting from cyclic eras. In this framework, prior cosmic events include cyclic matter-radiation-Big Bang periods and prior inflation.

Quantum theory can produce nonlocality in experiments with entangled particles measured simultaneously, assuming certain conditions about how measurements are chosen. However, some argue that these conditions about how measurements are chosen may not hold in the context of the theories that can explain the observed nonlocality. This leads researchers to explore the connections between these assumptions and nonlocality, as well as the observed features of the universe. This paper examines various theoretical frameworks for explaining the observed nonlocality, including a specific model based on a geometric arrangement of measurements and an alternative model based on combining multiple sets of measurements. These frameworks can explain the observed nonlocality, but they come with a cost: they rely on a different assumption about how measurements are chosen, one that differs from the original assumption in a subtle yet significant way. This paper examines these frameworks, their capabilities, and their connections to empirical tests, leading researchers to consider the possibility that the observed nonlocality may rely on a different assumption about how measurements are chosen, one that differs from the original assumption in a way that can be tested empirically.

The exponential growth in the size of neural networks poses significant challenges for their deployment on memory and computation-constrained devices such as smart speakers, wearables, and mobile phones. To address this issue, researchers have developed novel algorithms for quantizing neural network weights, which involve directly modeling their singular value decomposition (SVD) structure to reduce storage requirements. This paper delves deeper into this direction by formulating a theoretical framework for SVD-based quantization, analyzing the impact of SVD truncation and low-precision encoding on model accuracy, and providing a practical method for SVD-based quantization based on low-rank approximation. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in maintaining model accuracy while significantly reducing storage needs.

Building on previous research, we extended our analysis of cluster expansions for the dimer model to include isoradial graphs using the matching of cluster expansions, both on the graph and its dual, along its matching lattice counterparts. This facilitated a precise identification, term by term, of cluster expansions on both the original graph and its dual isoradial lattice. Consequently, we established a complex identity that connects the dimer model on isoradial graphs to its dual, taking into account a specific set of conditions. Our findings have multiple applications, one of which is the derivation of a compact formula for the partition function of isoradial graphs that closely mirrors the formula developed for planar graphs. Another significant implication is the derivation of a compact formula for the probability of a given dimer configuration. Additionally, we provide new proofs for the equilibrium properties of dimers on these isoradial graphs.

In a linear regression model with continuous or categorical data, a univariate Gaussian distribution is typically assigned to the conditional mean of the response variable given the covariates. However, a high-dimensional setting where the number of parameters exceeds the number of observations leads to identifiability issues, which can be addressed using penalized algorithms. The Group Lasso algorithm is used for variable selection, but it requires prior grouping information. We consider a data-driven approach to group variables based on pairwise correlations, and then apply the Group Lasso algorithm. We demonstrate that this method produces consistent variable selection, and it is shown through simulation studies that it handles both continuous and categorical data effectively, including interactions.

Embedded systems within vehicles, such as those found in automated driving and in-depth monitoring, have increasingly stringent requirements for both real-time performance and data security, often conflicting with each other. A proposed solution, T-Visor, is a real-time virtualization framework that enables the coexistence of time-critical and data-critical applications within the same system. It achieves this by introducing a two-level virtualization structure, where a trusted virtualization layer isolates and manages multiple virtual machines, each corresponding to an application with distinct needs. The framework employs isolated device drivers to control resource access, ensuring that time-critical virtual machines have exclusive access to essential resources. In this manner, T-Isor effectively enforces strict timing guarantees while also providing enhanced security for embedded systems within the automotive industry.

Many mobile panoramic imaging systems utilize inertial measurement units to efficiently capture images, given the imaging devices' inherent limitations in rotational speed. To develop a realistic simulation of panoramic imaging, we've created a novel IMU-based image capture model that simulates the rotational movement of the imaging device, given the limitations in rotational velocity. This model enables a new algorithm to generate synthetic panoramic images, utilizing auto-generated synthetic scenes. As a result, we've developed a comprehensive dataset of panoramic images and synthetic images, which have been used to train and assess panoramic stitching algorithms, yielding improved results in real-world image stitching tasks.

A study examining a network of Kuramoto oscillators, where a significant number of incoherent nodes are connected to a smaller, already coherent cluster, both in a heterogenous and homogenous setting. Results show that, contrary to the general understanding, increasing differences among the incoherent nodes does not necessarily make the two-state solution less stable, and in fact, it's the variation within the fully coherent cluster that tends to destabilize a network. However, when it comes to the variation within the incoherent group, increased diversity does not always lead to a two-state solution's destabilization.

Reinforcement learning methods that utilize value functions to predict future rewards are increasingly being applied to control tasks, yet they often overlook the underlying dynamics of the environment. This paper introduces dynamic reinforcement learning, a technique that incorporates both a value function and a conditionally probability density model of future states. By enforcing a noise floor in the dynamics model, we found that it can be leveraged to develop robust controllers that are less sensitive to perturbations. This approach was demonstrated through experiments on a simulated cartpole, which showed that it can learn controllers that are more resilient to observation noise and model misspecification than traditional methods.
We establish the connections between matrix and tensor algebras on the one hand, and the slice algebra construction on quivers on the other hand, employing an computer-aided approach.

A novel random tensor network model is proposed, where the network is segmented into two areas and is split into two sub-networks, reflecting a spectral component. The model is further developed by creating an analog to the typical R'enyi spectrum but for the reflected entanglement spectrum. The entangled state in the reflected spectrum is distinct due to its representation as a reflection of the random tensor network state. The cross-over behavior between low and high disorder is analyzed and a theoretical framework is proposed to describe this phenomenon. The non-monotonic behavior of the reflected entanglement spectrum is observed in contrast to the R'enyi spectrum and is attributed to the entanglement with the medium.

This study investigates the likelihood of long-term stability within ensembles of complex dynamical systems. The approach involves adapting the $q$-generalized entropy method to develop a multi-dimensional measure of stability that accounts for the dynamics of individual system components. By applying this method to well-known dynamical systems such as Lorenz, Rossler, and Lorenz-96, we develop a novel metric for persistence probability as a function of $q$ and system state. The results reveal that a specific range of $q$ values corresponds to the optimal description of persistence probabilities, and that changes in system conditions can affect optimal $q$. The findings also demonstrate a transition between different probability distribution types based on the system's control parameters, and highlight the significance of initial conditions near the boundary of non-stable attractors.

We establish a novel framework for analyzing the topological features of phase space in quadratic maps of the form $f_\mu$ with parameter $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$. By examining quadratic diffeomorphisms, we show that stable and unstable manifolds of periodic orbits partition the diffeomorphism's parameter space into separate regions, each sharing the same phase space topology. We extend this approach to Lorenz systems, grouping systems based on the topological equivalence of their phase space structures.

Recent studies in gravity have shown that holonomy is not consistent with gauge theory approaches. Instead, holonomy in gravity is determined by the presence of non-metricity. This implies that the gravitational variables, connection and metric, exhibit a distinct behavior that sets them apart. Consequently, the loop space of connection and metric forms a gauge orbit. To address this discrepancy, a novel constraint is introduced, known as Wilson loop non-invariance, as a potential gravitational counterpart to Yang-Mills theory. This new constraint, when applied to quantum gravity, enables the transition from spin networks to group field theory, ultimately leading to a coherent Lagrangian formulation.

This research focuses on the behavior of cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) and probability density functions (PDFs) of the random variables U_n and V_n derived from uniform random variables. By employing a simple method, we can show that the CDFs of U_n and V_n converge to the Heaviside step function as n increases, with the convergence occurring uniformly. Moreover, using the Leibniz rule, we derive the convergence behavior of the PDFs of U_n and V_n in the even and odd cases respectively. The related findings for the U_n even case can be extended to the U_n odd case through a straightforward transformation. The analogous results for the random variables W_n hold true and are presented in a similar manner. The specific PDF calculation for the random variable Z_3 is also outlined.

The proposed actual tunneling time (ATT) is directly linked to the current density, which is also the inverse of tunneling density of states (TDOS). Unlike the AFDT, the new ATT accounts for tunneling particles' spin fluctuations, which are not included in the existing tunneling theory. A simulation of ATTDOS was conducted in a double tunnel junction (DTJ) structure using a two-dimensional spin-dependent non-equilibrium Green's function (SDNEGF) method. The results revealed that the TDOS is influenced by magnetic field strength and tunnel barrier thickness. Furthermore, the SDNEGF-based simulation demonstrated that the ATT is directly related to spin fluctuations, particularly in specific energy regions. A numerical evaluation of the spin-dependent phase shift in DTG, influenced by magnetic field and tunnel barrier parameters, was presented. A theoretical model of spin-dependent electron transport in a magnetoelectronic device was presented, accounting for the temperature-dependent phase shift in the magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ). A numerical study of the temperature-dependent phase shift in MTJ was conducted, and the results showed a notable phase shift, which is dependent on the magnetic layer's thickness. A numerical study of the temperature-dependent phase shift in MTJ was conducted, and the results showed a notable phase shift, which is dependent on the magnetic layer's thickness.

A detailed examination of the impact of relativistic corrections on the
amplitudes of P-wave charmonia mesons, computed within the light-cone QCD sum rules
method, has been conducted. Our findings show that these corrections significantly
affect the form factors and their corresponding amplitudes of P-wave charmonia
mesons. Furthermore, our calculations reveal that the leading-order relativistic
corrections to the six-type amplitudes of ${}^3\mathrm{S}_1$ P-wave charmonia
mesons are substantial, ranging from 10% to 30%, while the influence of these
corrections becomes less pronounced at higher orders of the perturbative expansion.
In addition, our results demonstrate that the contributions from the six-type
amplitudes of ${}^3\mathrm{S}_1$ P-wave charmonia mesons are real.

Ramsey interferometry is a highly accurate measurement technique that is extensively used in quantum sensing. Its precision is typically limited by standard quantum noise, which can be surpassed by employing a non-linear phase shift. Here, we present an alternative approach to create such an experiment by utilizing a Bose-Einstein condensate and a nonlinear Hadamard gate, which enhances the sensitivity of the interferometry to reach the Heisenberg limit. Moreover, our model demonstrates the ability to distinguish between two closely spaced atom masses within the quantum noise level.

The research explores the linearized gravitational modes in the $e$BMS algebra, which describes asymptotically flat spacetime in 2+1 dimensions with massive particles. By decomposing the asymptotic Einstein equation, a scalar theory with a massive particle emerges, exhibiting first-order dynamics. The findings reveal a significant mass degeneracy in the $e$BMS charges, with the second component having a wider range than the first. This degeneracy in the vacua has connections to the concepts of soft news and the Schwarzian mode, thereby extending previous findings on the eBMS vacua to incorporate the scenario with a massive particle.

Deep neural networks have achieved impressive accuracy across various domains, but they often struggle with the issue of overfitting. To mitigate this problem, ensemble methods have shown considerable success. This research introduces an efficient ensemble approach that can train multiple networks simultaneously, reducing the time required for training to that of a single network, by leveraging shared pre-fitting data. The technique involves using data pre-selected via a fitness function to accelerate convergence and shares intermediate calculations among the networks, thereby enhancing performance. The proposed method outperforms traditional ensemble techniques in multiple datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR10, and ImageNet.

A connection with a generalized connection is used to define a connection on a smooth generalized complex structure on an even-dimensional manifold. This concept leads to new generalized connections that correspond to self-dual and anti-self-dual Ricci-flat metrics in specific scenarios. This work also establishes conditions for the existence of generalized K\"ahler metrics that meet certain constraints.

The researchers investigate polynomial mappings over finite fields, particularly focusing on complete mappings and their connections to the Malfatti cubes. They also explore computationally infeasible cases, such as mappings over prime power fields with no solutions.

A novel, automated visual method for detecting intestinal parasites in fecal samples is presented. Due to the limitations of human-based diagnosis, particularly the high error rates associated with visual inspection, this system aims to provide a reliable alternative. The framework combines two deep learning components: a convolutional neural network and a point set neural network, which work synergistically to identify parasites within the images. The framework first utilizes a CNN to classify whether an fecal image contains a parasite, and if so, employs a PSNet to pinpoint the parasite's location and shape. The PSNet's ability to efficiently process the spatial information of the parasite also enables feature extraction, enhancing the overall performance of the system. The framework's performance was validated on a large dataset of 10000 images, collected from 100 individuals, resulting in a remarkably low false positive and false negative rate of 0.01% for both the initial classification and the regression tasks.

This research investigates the non-linear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations of the continuum L^\infty control problem, a concept introduced by Friedman in his 1981 publication. We derive the viscosity solution of this equation by integrating two approaches: the compactness method for approximating the L^\infty control problem, and the comparison principle for approximating coupled non-linear Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations with constant Hamiltonians. It is worth noting that the solution of the L^\infty control problem can be seen as a combination of these two principles. Moreover, we establish a link between the viscosity solution of the nonlinear integro-differential equation and an optimal control problem, thereby providing a meaningful interpretation for the viscosity solution of the nonlinear integro-differential equation.

This study introduces a novel control approach, known as the Genetic Filter (GF), tailored for quadcoter systems. GF integrates the adaptive capabilities of evolutionary algorithms to optimize controller and filter parameters concurrently. We demonstrate the GF's robustness against disturbances by comparing its performance against a conventional Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) based controller. Utilizing a Simulink model representing an actual quadcopter, the GF's efficacy is showcased, with results indicating its ability to swiftly counteract disturbances and outperform LQR in various scenarios.

A status update on the Lattice QCD calculation for the pion-nucleon sigma term will be provided, which is relevant to both particle and nuclear physics as well as to the dark matter search. Recent developments in the computation will be discussed, along with a lattice QCD calculation of the nucleon matrix element of the scalar form factor, as it is an essential component for accurately determining the sigma term. The ongoing efforts to reduce statistical uncertainties through the all-mode coupling acceleration and the external source method, as well as to reduce systematic uncertainties from finite volume effects and quark mass extrapolation, will be discussed. Additionally, an improvement in taste breaking will be expected from the highly optimized MELO width minimization approach. Current progress on calculating the disconnected diagrams using the stochastic source method and their expected impact on the sigma term calculation will also be presented.

The CMS silicon pixel detector upgrade project is in progress. The innermost layer of the detector was replaced in 2016, with further improvements scheduled for the near future. The replacement process began with a thorough analysis of the initial detector's operation. The new CMS pixel detector will comprise three layers utilizing advanced technology, including thin detection panels and highly efficient sensors. The latest findings on the detector's development and implementation will be presented here.

We have developed an advanced, automated system for identifying Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) host galaxies in the SDSS-III/IV MaNGA survey. Leveraging the SkyNet deep learning network, the system achieves high precision in classifying 10,754 MaNGA targets. It excels in accuracy for galaxies at redshifts less than 0.15, but is most effective in identifying distant objects. Furthermore, the system's accuracy is not hindered by variations in galaxy size or distance. Furthermore, the system's accuracy is bolstered by the addition of two new features derived from the Star Formation Rate (SFR) maps of SkyNet's output. Furthermore, the system's predictions are in harmony with previous research, revealing a notable increase in the number of AGN at higher redshifts. Furthermore, the system's predictions are in line with the observed relationship between the fraction of AGN and the redshift of the host galaxy.

The thickness of the nuclear skin for neutrons is influenced by short-range correlations between nuclei. An asymmetric neutron-proton slab model has been employed to study how these correlations impact neutron thickness. The results reveal that correlations can decrease the neutron thickness by up to 20%, with more significant interactions leading to a more pronounced reduction. The study also indicates that correlations can alter the asymmetry of the neutron thickness, whereas they may not affect the asymmetry of the proton thickness. Additionally, the density at which the neutron thickness is measured is found to be lower than the central density, suggesting that experiments focused on this region could be more sensitive to correlations. The overall findings imply that precise measurements of neutron thickness could help researchers better understand the effects of short-range correlations in the nucleus.

This paper presents computational experiments evaluating the effects of the RGB image representation on the performance of supervised color transfer learning algorithms. An unsupervised method for color transfer is also introduced and tested. The quality of the transferred color is assessed through the histogram intersection metric and metrics measuring hue shift and color channel correlation, all of which demonstrate significant improvement with the new RGB image representation. Furthermore, the proposed representation facilitates color transfer in cases where traditional methods fail, including the transfer of textures and transparency effects. The novel representation is also capable of transferring complex color information from natural images to synthetic images. The proposed unsupervised method does not rely on a reference image database.

The relationship between geometrical scaling and gluon distribution saturation is 
exhibited in experimental findings across multiple reactions. The quark-Gluon 
Compton scattering process is studied to demonstrate the application of the 
saturation model. Additionally, the rapidity density of one-photon two-electron 
production is analyzed with an eye towards possible saturation effects.

The early galaxy's enrichment by core-collapse supernovae is examined, with a focus on how the progenitor masses are randomly sampled, given the known mass distribution. An analytical method is proposed to calculate the distribution of iron and nickel produced in the resulting supernovae, based on the distribution of the random variables. This approach accurately captures the predicted mean, standard deviation, and skewness of the produced elements. The stochasticity in the enrichment process is found to be significant, with the predicted distribution of iron and nickel in the early galaxy showing substantial variations. This has implications for the interpretation of r-process elements in the early galaxy, particularly in the case of heavy elements like osmium, iridium, and platinum.

A common data analysis practice involves enhancing predictive models by combining existing explanatory variables with synthetic ones derived from historical models. We investigate how this process affects model stability, demonstrating that increased stability corresponds to decreased bias in predicting future outcomes, particularly when additional predictors are incorporated. Based on this relationship, our study derives data-driven criteria for identifying the optimal synthetic predictor that optimally balances model bias and variance. We also conduct both simulated and real-world experiments to validate the efficacy of our findings, showing that the suggested approach yields superior predictive outcomes.

This paper investigates the computational efficiency of gradient calculations in variational quantum models, focusing on the role of the output. We examine two types of outputs - expectation values and probabilities - and demonstrate that the commonly used parameter-shift rule for expectation values is essentially the only feasible method for large-scale optimization. In contrast, we show that computing gradients of probabilities can be done efficiently, even for complex circuits, by leveraging a straightforward definition of the derivative. Our approach is to represent quantum circuits as directed graphs, allowing for the calculation of gradients by summing a small number of terms. Our findings suggest that optimizing quantum circuits with outputs that are not expectation values may be a more practical approach, given current technological limitations.

This paper focuses on identifying pointwise semi-slant submanifolds within Sasakian manifolds and characterizing warped product submanifolds as either lightlike or maximal, ultimately discovering that such points exist and either constitute a lightlike warped product or a specific type of Riemannian submanifold.

Researchers at the DAne detector have made the most sensitive direct measurement of coherent elastic neutrino nucleus scattering to date, achieving this milestone by collecting 124.2 Neutrino-Megaton-Neutron-Joules of data from KARMNEUT experiment. Achieving this milestone involved combining a large 33 ton detector with a strong 5.35 kGp effective area, which enabled the detection of 1660 coherent events across various incoming neutrino energy ranges. This measurement aligns with standard model predictions, covering a range of 90% confidence intervals of cross-sections, spanning from 1.0 to 130 picobarns, and validating the neutrino's weak interaction coupling to quarks to a precision of 0.13.

Active dimers with a specific internal interaction can emulate Steerable Diodes when moving through an obstacle course of barriers. The combination of shape-selective interactions and active forces allows one internal state to experience rotational control similar to a steering wheel seen in macroscopic devices, whereas moving through power stroke dimers results in preferred direction traversal. The movement of such particles can exhibit various directed motion patterns, including unidirectional rotation, when adjusted based on internal state coupling.

This research examines the role of magnetoroton chirality within a single layer of electrons under a strong magnetic field. Notably, in in-plane magnetic fields, certain fractional quantum Hall states display a finite rotors chirality, with the most prominent instance being in a strong correlation regime where the lowest chirality state is observed. Chirality within the $
u=2/7$ state is compared to that of $
u=2/9$, with the former exhibiting a higher value. Furthermore, the study reveals that magnetoroton chirality is present in the $
u=2/7$ state despite its even denominator, with the chirality of the rotors being the driving force behind a strong correlation between the two states, with a theoretical value of the chirality of the rotors being in agreement with a derived formula.

A simple two-type Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) epidemic model is proposed, considering two distinct population groups with separate networks for physical and social interactions. The model incorporates an imperfect vaccine, which reduces the infected population's transmission rate but offers partial immunity. Through mathematical analysis, our model demonstrates relaxation of a specific population division into distinct classes of partial immunity. Consequently, arbitrary contact networks can be effectively partitioned into manageable subgroups, simplifying complex epidemic dynamics. We further explore particular network topologies, such as mixed and directed regular networks, to identify conditions promoting epidemic extinction and the emergence of stable endemic equilibria.

Bispectral bias in CMB maps arises from estimators that utilize frequency channels with non-uniform noise properties. This method is particularly suited for experiments where individual sources are masked out at specific frequency channels due to these uneven noises. Biais et al. demonstrated that the BICorr estimator effectively eliminates bias in CMB maps. This study investigates how CMB map bias and error are affected when strong point sources are present. It is observed that CMB map errors exhibit asymmetry when sources are masked at certain frequency channels, whereas using BICorr eliminates both bias and asymmetry. This study also examines scenarios where sources are masked in specific directions, revealing the impact on bias and asymmetry, and the potential for mitigating asymmetry through the BICorr estimator.

The rapid advancement of large language models has led to a significant increase in the adoption of task instruction scenarios for model evaluation and deployment. However, traditional instruction tuning relies on static, pre-compiled datasets, which can be insufficient to capture the dynamic and evolving nature of real-world tasks. This research presents an innovative method called real-world instruction gathering, which utilizes large language models to collect diverse and relevant task instructions directly from users in various contexts, weighted by task importance. The proposed approach demonstrates that incorporating pedantic elements and pragmatic considerations in instruction tuning can lead to improved task performance, and that the collected instructions can contribute to a dynamic and diverse set of public instructions, expanding the availability of traditional static datasets. The proposed method has been successfully demonstrated through multiple real-world tasks, including a chatbot for a museum, a chaperone for a chemo patient, and a child-friendly search engine, where incorporating user Pedagogical feedback resulted in more effective and efficient model performance.

A new technique called shadow tomography can determine multiple quantum states using a single state preparation, in contrast to traditional quantum state tomography which requires numerous state preparations. Shadow tomography measures numerous copies of the same quantum state, $\rho$, to obtain an approximate representation of each of $N$ different states $\sigma_i$. The technique relies on randomly applying Clifford unitaries $U$ to the states before measuring them, requiring $O(\log N)$ measurements to achieve an error rate of $O(1/\sqrt{m})$ for all $N$ predictions. This method has been found to efficiently reconstruct partial states even when the full state is unknown, allowing the prediction of specific properties of the quantum state $\rho$. Shadow tomography can also be performed using smaller neural network quantum optimizers (CNNQOs) despite their smaller size, enabling measurements of arbitrary CNNQO states despite a known density matrix. Shadow tomography has practical applications in quantum machine learning and benchmarking quantum devices.

For a strictly convex shape in the plane, we denote its incircle and circumcircle radii as $r$ and $R$, and its boundary as a piecewise smooth curve $\gamma$. If $\eta$ represents the smaller angle between these two circles, and the smaller arc of the circumcircle between their points of intersection is called $\sigma$, then a new proof of a theorem related to Bell's inequality is derived, stating that $\int_{\gamma} ds \leq \pi(R^2-R^2/4)\left(\frac{1}{rR}\int_{\sigma} s ds + \frac{1}{2}\right)$, where $s$ is the distance from the center of the incircle to a point on the boundary, and this proof relies on a known inequality concerning the perimeter of a convex shape.

This study presents a novel algorithm for optimal path planning in mobile UAV networks to maximize the number of served users while adhering to a path length limit, which corresponds to a complex problem variation with numerous constraints. To address this challenge, the research utilizes an improved greedy strategy based on a tree data structure that efficiently solves this path optimization issue. Notably, the constructed tree guarantees the existence of an optimal solution within a specific subset of feasible options, given certain conditions, and this research expands upon these findings to develop the new algorithm with improved computational efficiency. Simulation outcomes validate that the proposed algorithm achieves comparable results to a genetic algorithm, but with significantly reduced computational complexity.

We have developed a model for describing the behavior of nanoscale lattices when subjected to a quench process across a phase transition from a normal state to a state with nematic properties. In the latter state, we have found that the inherent symmetry of the lattice rotation is reduced to C2, and the normal state exhibits significant amplitude modulation. We have found that, in order to satisfy the quench process boundary conditions, the resulting domain pattern to form is limited to two dimensions. We have also discovered that, in a general case, these domains cannot be easily resolved into equilibrium states achievable without an external energy input input. We have found that a energy dissipation process occurs due to the quench process, and we have proposed a numerical energy minimization algorithm to obtain a final energy state that is in equilibrium with the system. We have further investigated an alternative energy minimization process that arises from a natural coarsening mechanism and found that it leads to a self-similar evolution of domain patterns. We have also proposed an analytical model to describe this evolution and found that it is consistent with the simulation results.

The conformation of endofullerene molecules significantly affects the transfer of their quantum properties to a solid-state environment. Research conducted in a study reveals how the arrangement of carbon atoms within an $C_{60}$ molecule embedded in a substrate impacts the magnetic and electric behavior when a spin-qubit is nearby. The shape of the fullerene can either amplify or diminish the qubit's sensitivity to its surroundings, including instances where the spin-qubit becomes localized in a cluster of electrons created by a defect in the substrate. The behavior of this qubit can be manipulated by modifying the fullerene's conformation, offering a mechanism for control.

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things has brought about heightened worries about data security and confidentiality. As a result, there is a growing need for more secure authentication and privacy protection measures within IoT systems. Existing approaches to confidentiality, such as encryption, are often costly and time-consuming, making them less ideal for IoT devices. This has led to increased interest in physical layer security methods, which leverage the inherent security of communication channels. This paper presents a novel approach to security, involving both devices and users, where devices contribute to the identification of suspicious users. This collaborative method, known as device-assisted physical layer security, combines the benefits of device-level and user-level security systems. The authors propose a game-theoretic framework that optimizes the overall network security by having devices and users collaborate through a price-setting mechanism. This game-theoretic approach allows for the identification of a system-wide stable state, known as the Nash equilibrium, which represents the optimal security configuration for all participants.

To assess the optimal Bayesian experiment design against adaptive and random strategies, BOLD's efficacy is tested via simulations of low-fidelity Ramsey measurements. The design's parameters, frequency offset and bin timing, are optimized within unknown parameters and fixed coherence time. The goal is to accurately estimate an offset frequency to minimize drift. The simulations show that Bayesian design outperforms adaptive and random methods, achieving lower uncertainty, especially with limited measurement time or unknown initial conditions.

Network centrality is a well-established method used to identify the relative importance of nodes within a graph-based network. Many centrality metrics have been proposed over the years, each tailored to a specific type of network or tailored to a particular aspect of a node's influence. However, the sheer number of available centrality measures can be overwhelming for researchers, making it difficult to choose the most suitable one for a given application. In this research, we aim to introduce a novel network centrality measure known as "Gromov centrality". This centrality is applicable to weighted graphs and measures a node's importance based on the average distance to the most significant portion of the graph. Our experimental findings indicate that Gromov centrality can effectively distinguish between different kinds of nodes across various generated networks. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of combining Gromov centrality with other centrality measures, such as betweenness centrality, to achieve even better results. Ultimately, our research aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the Gromov centrality's performance across a wide range of networks generated under different parameters.

Building on the assumptions of a particular theory, this work seeks to validate them through experimental findings. We utilized data from laser ranging to measurements of the Moon and demonstrated that one key hypothesis of the theory is consistent with these results. Additionally, our analysis shows that the theory can adequately explain the observed gradual increase in the Moon's distance from the Earth over time. We derived specific values for certain theoretical constants related to Newton's law, which were found to be consistent with existing measurements of planetary motion within a specified level of uncertainty. We derived two equations that describe the relationship between a planet's orbital period and semi-major axis, and using these, we determined that the uncertainty in a particular constant is approximately 0.023. We further established equations that relate to the orbital characteristics of planets and satellites, providing expressions for their eccentricities, inclinations, and other properties. We specifically calculated the changes in the perigee and node of a satellite orbiting a planet, demonstrating that the uncertainty in a particular constant affecting these equations is roughly 0.0000001. We also derived an equation that describes the relationship between a planet's mean motion and other celestial bodies in its solar system, showing that the uncertainty in a particular constant affecting this equation is approximately 0.000000000000000000000000000000000000000000

It is demonstrated that this condition number is an open set within its closure, with respect to properties related to the spectrum of these polynomials. Furthermore, a characterization of its closure within the space of all matrix polynomials, which includes those that satisfy a similar condition, is derived. Additionally, this work provides a detailed examination of this condition in the context of specific types of matrix polynomials, including those that describe periodic linear differential equations and spectral polynomials, which are used to describe periodic operators and symmetric multiplication operators with gaps in their respective spectra. In a comprehensive examination of continuous-trace algebras, a thorough check is performed to assess their suitability as generalized G-branes, which requires them to satisfy certain hoisted multicenter conditions for non-geometric strings. This assessment ultimately reveals that only a very limited number of continuous-trace algebras meet the criteria, which significantly constrains the existence of generalized G-branes and, in turn, the potential for non-geometric string multistrand dynamics and classical T-duals.

Our proposed embedding method can efficiently map $H$ to $G$ within a factor of $(1+\varepsilon)$, where $H$ is a graph with no minor of size more than $k$, and $G$ is a graph with treewidth at most $k^\Omega(k)$. This results in the computation complexity of $(n+m)k^O(k)$. This allows us to achieve a significant improvement in the efficiency of several algorithms for metric Baker's problems in minor-free graphs, specifically reducing the computational complexity from $(nk)^O(k)$ to $(n+m)k^O(k)$. This also enables us to present faster algorithms for Baker's problems, such as those for shortest paths and related problems, with improved computational complexity and approximation ratios.

Research has been conducted to understand the impact of varying initial conditions on the asymptotic behavior of solutions to a time-periodic diffusion equation, focusing particularly on the scenario involving a nonlinear reaction and a Dirichlet boundary condition. The study reveals that the asymptotic state is ultimately periodic, sharing the same period as the forcing function in the equation, yet its amplitude oscillates based on initial conditions that fall within a non-empty, nonlinear functional space. Notably, the set of initial conditions leading to divergent or non-periodic solutions also exists. By utilizing a nonlinear transformation, the study demonstrates the existence of a periodic solution with a unique minimal period and uniform asymptotic stability. The results also show that solutions to a modified version of the equation, with Neumann boundary conditions, exhibit similar properties.

The real-time optimization framework known as ADAPT-VQE, originally tailored for quantum simulators handling fermionic systems, has been adapted for quantum computers operating on qubits. We introduce a modified protocol, qubit-based ADAPT-VQE (QEB-ADAPT-VQE), that enhances the speed of convergence compared to both the original version adapted for qubits. This updated version is capable of automatically selecting the type of quantum gates necessary for implementation and incorporates an algorithm to minimize the required gate operations when finding a specific target state. It has been tested using quantum computers simulating fermionic systems, including those employing automatic differentiation, and has shown the ability to compete with the original version adapted for qubits in a short period of time, even without using specialized techniques to reduce error rates, while also demonstrating the capacity to choose the optimal set of quantum gates to use during optimization.

A deep unsupervised learning method called Deep Generative Decoder (DGD) has been developed to represent data in a designated space without any pre-existing labels. The DGD achieves class separation by initially forcing labeled data points to map to a predetermined cluster center and by training the model to minimize the distance between data points within the same class. The DGD uses a three-part structure consisting of a feature extractor, cluster predictor, and generative decoder. The first component maps input data to a latent space, while the cluster predictor generates a prediction for each input data point, and the generative decoder maps this prediction back to the original input space. The DGD has been tested with two distinct datasets and has demonstrated superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

This study examines the potential of incorporating a stiff component into the cosmological model to address both the Hubble tension and the cosmological constant problem. Utilizing a specific version of the Brans-Dicke theory, we investigate whether its scalar field can give rise to a stiff component capable of mitigating the cosmological constant. Our analysis reveals that while this scenario offers a dynamic solution to the cosmological constant problem, it fails to alleviate the Hubble tension for a scalar field stiff component. Conversely, introducing a stiff fluid with equation of state w=1 effectively resolves both issues under certain parameter constraints, specifically H0<77km/s/Mpc and the Brans-Dicke parameter not exceeding the value of 6.

We examined the spatial distribution of 13 molecules in Comet C/2015 ER61 using 36 maps, which enabled us to determine the spatial profiles of H$_2$CO, HNC, CH$_3$OH, CS, CO, SiS, H$_2$S, HCN, SO, NH$_3$, N$_2$, N$_2$H, and N$_2$H$_2$. Notably, HCN was found to be significantly more active than other molecules, with its outgassing extending 10 times further than the others. Our results indicate that, with a few exceptions, the comet's outgassing is best described by a non-volatile sublimation model. The measured velocity of outgassing was 1.0-1.2 times 10$^5$ cm s$^{-1}$, which aligns with the theoretical value for gas escaping due to ice sublimation driven by solar heating. The notable exception of HCN, however, could be attributed to the presence of more volatile precursors such as N$_2$ or CH$_4$.

A novel approach for speech synthesis without supervision is proposed, utilizing voice onboarding without requiring speech training. Voice onboarding is achieved without supervision by leveraging laryngeal feature extraction. Furthermore, the framework for unsupervised speech synthesis with no prior speech data is developed. As a result, speech synthesis without supervision only relies on laryngeal features for no prior speech data exists. Evaluated using the RIMES voice onboarding dataset, laryngeal features enhance the synthesized speech ratings, yet still fall short of supervised systems in terms of both naturalness and clarity. Nevertheless, the increase in rating from unsupervised to non-speech data systems indicates that the generated speech is more akin to its corresponding voice onboarding pattern, with the potential for further systems refinement.

We've investigated the one-loop effective potential of the Tsallis holographic dark energy model with a negative potential cutoff, $l$, and discovered its one-loop effective potential takes a similar form to its zeroth-order potential. Notably, the interacting coupling parameter $\theta$ is connected to the constant parameter $b^2$ in the original model, with $\theta \propto (1/b)^4$. Furthermore, the effective potential's form and its dependence on the interplay between $\theta$ and $b$ are consistent across the entire model's negative potential cutoff range, with the effective potential's form and its logarithmic nature aligning with those of the Callan-Coleman-Sweet model.

In real-world applications, complex and large-scale optimisation problems are often encountered, necessitating the use of heuristic algorithms that can rapidly find near-optimal solutions. The choice of an appropriate heuristic algorithm depends on the specific optimisation problem at hand, and evaluating the quality of a solution requires a metric. The investment ratio (IR) metric measures how much better a solution is compared to a random one, and how much extra 'investment' is required to achieve that improvement. The IR metric is versatile, and can be applied to any optimisation problem, regardless of its type. The IR metric was used to compare solutions from the well-known genetic algorithm, and to evaluate the quality of a solution in the context of the maximum satisfiability problem.

This paper explores the concepts of source path and source simply connected groupoid within the context of synthetic differential geometry. We begin by establishing the properties and definitions, then proceed to generate the corresponding lemmas and propositions, ultimately creating a comprehensive overview based on user-defined assumptions.

This paper introduces Dynaswap, a DeFi-based exchange platform that prioritizes
security through the integration of multi-signature functionality, smart contract
audits, and Zero Knowledge Proofs. Dynaswap allows users to create custom exchange
amounts and prices, incorporating Multi-sig exchanges, custom ZKP, and providing
transparency via Dynaswap Explorer. Additionally, the platform features developer
documentation and a CMS panel for managing node validators. Dynaswap's architecture
is broken down into its core components, with a focus on its multi-signature system
utilizing CredItVk, its custom platform contract, and its Dynaswap Explorer based on
IPFS and Vue.js.

This research addresses the SPO task by introducing a supervised contrastive pre-training approach that enables models to effectively capture sentence sentence's sentiment orientation through contrastive learning. The traditional pre-training methods, which rely on masked language modeling, fail to take into account the sentiment nuances in reviews. The proposed method supplements the standard masked language modeling with the supervision of contrastive sentiment learning, thereby enabling the model to efficiently encode the semantic and sentiment features of sentences during pre-training. Extensive experiments conducted on the SPO benchmark using the GLUE suite have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach, resulting in 3.0% and 5.2% improvements in single-tower and dual-tower contrastive learning methods, respectively.

Gastric acid suppression increases the risk of contracting listeriosis, an infection caused by Listeria monocytogenes.  Most studies have attributed this increased risk to the survival and multiplication of L. monocytogenes in food storage environments. However, this research proposes an alternative explanation, suggesting that the increased risk is a result of reduced immune system function in the host. A mathematical model was developed to investigate this hypothesis, taking into account the production of bicarbonate by the host in response to L. monocytogenes infection. Model simulations showed that the increased risk of listeriosis following gastric acid suppression is a result of decreased host immune system function, as measured by bicarbonate production rates. Furthermore, the model demonstrated that the host's ability to clear L. monocytogenes infections declines as the duration of gastric acid suppression increases. Our findings indicate that the increased risk of listeriosis following gastric acid suppression is a result of reduced host immune system function, an effect that could be mitigated in future by further research and development of novel therapies.

This study examines the impact of hardware limitations in secure communication systems using reconfigurable intelligent surfaces. We analyze two key hardware constraints in these systems: phase quantization in the reflective elements and nonlinear distortion in the transmitted signals. By formulating the optimal beamforming and phase-shift strategies to maximize weighted sum secrecy rates under both distortions, we show that these hardware constraints significantly reduce secrecy rates. We also develop a non-linear optimization model to determine the best values for these parameters, and leverage phase shift linearization to simplify the problem into a more manageable form. By using successive convex approximation, we obtain the optimal solution and compare it with a suboptimal method, revealing the substantial performance loss due to these hardware constraints.

This theory posits two forms of summarization: hindsight and prediction. When examining the prediction summarization process, our theory posits that minimizing prediction errors involves creating high-level summaries that represent the primary patterns in sensory input. In contrast, our theory posits that minimizing attended prediction errors involves creating low-level summaries that represent the primary patterns in predicted sensory inputs. This theory posits that minimizing these errors, both in the past and future, drives learning and leads to adaptive behaviors. A comprehensive review of solar wind energy distribution research is presented, focusing on datasets from various heights in the solar atmosphere and distance from the sun's center. The energy distribution observations are compared to the classic Taitz equation, a gold standard for our current understanding of the solar wind, at 1 AU. The review reveals that solar wind energy distribution at 1 AU adheres to a kappa distribution with a value of approximately 4, reflecting the balance between heating and cooling processes. The review also highlights the significant role of electron-ion temperature differences in the solar wind, caused by charge separation effects, and notes that charge separation may not be a viable explanation for this phenomenon. The review's data suggest that solar energy distribution changes significantly at heights below 0.1 solar radius, deviating from observations at 1 AU.

In the context of groupoid C*-algebras, this paper examines various forms of relative freeness. We demonstrate that one such condition is equivalent to the freeness of a specific action on a G-C*-algebra. Moreover, this type of freeness corresponds with other established C*-algebra constructions, including full and reduced crossed products. Under a specific assumption, we show that further types of relative freeness correspond to freeness of graded C*-algebras. We also explore examples of relative freeness, including the case of tree actions. Notably, this study reveals a key distinction between relative freeness and exactness.

In P. Simon's work, the concept of $P$-points from cardinal arithmetic is extended to include an analogous notion for metric spaces. It is demonstrated that 2020 is the minimum possible year of consistency for the existence of a non-principal ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$ in conjunction with a $P$-year metric space. Moreover, under the assumption of GCH, it is proven that the minimal year of consistency for the existence of a metric $P$-space is 1360.

The paper examines the behavior of an open two-qubit system that's subject to mechanical vibrations and can be controlled through optical means. By incorporating a specific mathematical deformation into the model, it is possible to control how the quantum states interact. Researchers study the case where two different deformation parameters are involved, and they explore how this affects the probe field and signal transmission. By adjusting certain parameters, it is possible to control the phase behavior of the probe field and even achieve a longer-lasting connection between the quantum states that is not possible in the standard model.

A theoretical study has been conducted to analyze the characteristics of "scissors modes" in medium-weight nuclei, specifically in $^{106}$Ru and $^{108}$Ru. Calculations were performed using the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov method with a monopair interaction, the cranked shell model, and the RBC method. The study focused on examining features such as energy levels, wave functions, and electromagnetic transitions. The outcomes revealed that R-negative scissors modes are more sensitive to the choice of interaction than R-positive ones. The outcomes of the RBC calculations were found to be in good agreement with experimental data. The study also suggested that an excited negative parity scissors mode at 5.5 MeV in $^{106}$Ru could be associated with an assignment of 2$^-$ due to its strong electromagnetic transitions.

A research study investigates a nonlinear hyperbosity conservation law using data-driven methods in space. A neural network-based approach was tested for solving conservation laws, initially using the Euler equations as a reference point. The nonlinear conservation law was resolved with a neural network approach, comparing its efficacy against traditional finite volume methods. The results indicate that this method is capable of producing accurate results, including complex wave phenomena and contact discontinuities, without requiring additional stabilization. Furthermore, it was found that this network-based method exhibits improved accuracy compared to the traditional approach, including accurate shock and Riemann fan formations.

The Large Hadron Electron Collider, a hybrid electron-proton collider located at CERN, is scheduled to commence operations in 2029. This article provides an overview of the LS3 detector, which has played a significant role in deep-inelastic scattering experiments from the late 1980s to the early 1990s. In addition to detailing the current detector's features, we discuss proposed enhancements aimed at expanding LS3's research potential for future experiments. Specifically, these upgrades will allow the detector to explore smaller values of x, accurately measure cross-sections at low values of Q-squared, and gather precise data on the proton's altitudinal structure, particularly its gluon distribution.

This paper demonstrates how an evolving Lambda system can detect both the Unruh and Casimir effects. The detection mechanism for these phenomena is explained using the geometric framework of lambda systems with a time-dependent component. A specific scenario is examined to show that a specific configuration of a triple double well system can simultaneously reveal the Unruh and Casimir effects.

In English, effective Event Extraction is possible with established techniques, but they are not directly applicable to other languages. To facilitate event extraction in any language, we developed a novel method that utilizes a language model trained on the complete set of words in that language, along with a specific algorithm to identify potential events within it. By testing this method on 18 different languages, we discovered it to be effective in identifying events, even without prior knowledge of multi-word expressions. Additionally, our analysis revealed a significant correlation between language complexity and event extraction performance.

A previous study found the soft and hard band light curves of a high mass X-ray binary, H1743-325, are not synchronized, with a time lag of up to 10 minutes. We have analyzed the synchronization of these light curves in more detail, using our own 2019-2020 monitoring data and re-examining earlier data from 2013-2014 and 2016-2017. We discovered that the synchronization time lag is influenced by the state of the source, with the soft state showing a longer time lag than the hard state. We also found that the synchronization time lag is correlated with the average photon flux in the hard state. We have explained the in-phase coherence phase shift of up to 1200 seconds by considering the propagation of an impulse through a two-channel system, consisting of a hard channel and a soft channel, which can explain the observed synchronization time lag. We have also discussed the physical meaning of the in-phase coherence phase lag, which can be related to the properties of the accretion disk wind, including the mass accretion rate and the size of the wind's reservoir.

The effects of the non-abelian aether term significantly impact the Stefan-Boltzmann law, Boltzmann constant, and Stefan's constant, as well as gluon energy density, pressure, and the Gluon equation of state, which can be altered by the aether term such that it matches that of a classical gas. Moreover, the Gluon equation of state, energy density, and pressure are dependent on the volume and approach zero as the volume approaches infinity. Notably, the Gluon equation of state exhibits a maximum value of 2.25 for a specific aether configuration.

We suggest a unified model that considers both syntax and semantics in languages, observing that patterns that benefit parsing in English also benefit translation when applied to other languages, despite contrasting views on universality in languages. Through our analysis of diverse language corpora and parsing algorithms, we uncover that syntactic and semantic structures share a similar outward appearance but have different underlying origins. Furthermore, we document a external validation of the benefits of a single, general-purpose syntactic model that is optimized for parsing in English but performs well across multiple languages.

Mergers of compact objects produce radiatively powered transients with a wide variety of appearances, ranging in luminosity from 103 to 105 times the solar luminosity. Although short gamma-ray bursts and kilonovae are expected to be associated with these transients, it's possible that some transients occur without associated gamma-ray bursts. A two-star model of accretion has been developed to simulate the behavior of these transients, and the results indicate that the light curves of these transients are characterized by a rapid initial rise in luminosity, a gradual decline, and a plateau phase. The duration of the transient event is primarily determined by the amount of radioactive material involved, and the peak luminosity is primarily determined by the amount of material involved. The observed diversity in transient light curves can be attributed to a range in both the amount of radioactive material involved and the energy released during the transient event. The two-star model accurately reproduces the observed light curves of several transients, and the model can be used to predict the properties of other transients.
