This paper delves into the characteristic polynomial of the inverse of specific matrix types known as arrowhead matrices with constant last row. We also explore the Gau-Wu number, an extension of the arrow matrix inverse characteristic polynomial, which applies to a broader class of matrices. Furthermore, we find the general form of this number for any size and provide an alternate expression that involves the inverse of a larger tridiagonal matrix with a uniform trace. We devise a method to compute the inverse of more complex matrices: k-generalized arrow matrices. We derive both a characteristic polynomial for the inverse of these k-generalized arrow matrices and recurrences that govern the coefficients of this polynomial. We also find the inverse of the characteristic polynomial of the k-generalized arrow matrix itself.

The proper decay lengths of beauty and charm particles, along with other relevant data, have been studied using the ATLAS detector. Leveraging the LHCb detector's tracking precision, researchers calculated the mean proper decay lengths for these particles and other background sources. By fitting proper distance distributions, researchers determined the following values: 495+7/-6 micrometers for beauty particles, 307+14/-10 micrometers for charm particles, 1040+32/-25 micrometers for J/psi particles, 180+10/-7 micrometers for B+ mesons, 454+16/-14 micrometers for B0 mesons, and 250+13/-11 micrometers for B0* baryons. These statistical findings align with the predictions made by the Particle Data Group.

This research explores the topological aspects of multi-class segmentation, where multiple color categories coexist in a space. By treating each color class as a distinct region within a topological framework, our approach employs persistent homology to capture the interplay between these topological subspaces. A novel method for integrating and comparing the resulting persistence diagrams is developed, allowing boundary translocation to occur only when the diagram sizes are equivalent. A theoretical foundation for this integration method is established, demonstrating the key role of the $L_2$ distance measure. Furthermore, this research proposes using the developed metric for evaluating multi-class segmentation outcomes. By applying this evaluation method to the multi-class K-nearest neighbor classifier, our results demonstrate its effectiveness and superiority over established metrics for parameter tuning.

This study investigates power control strategies within large interference networks, focusing on binary power control where base stations operate at a maximum power level or remain inactive. An analysis of the performance of a greedy decentralized power control algorithm reveals that this binary power control can achieve near-optimal results, merely within 1 dB of the optimal解决方案. For a more extensive simulation, it is demonstrated that the proportion of binaries solutions close to or achieve the same optimal power output approaches 1 as the network size expands indefinitely.

This paper introduces a computational framework for risk assessment in the financial accounting field. Our methodology utilizes the theory of belief functions, specifically Dempster-Shafer mass functions, to quantify the varying risks associated with accounts. This approach enables the representation of Bel(A) ≤ 1, indicating that the sum of the belief in the accounts' correctness and the potential for undetected errors in the accounts' summaries is equal to one. This risk assessment framework forms the foundation of a risk-based auditing system, where the Bel(A) value is used to determine the level of scrutiny applied to each account's accuracy.

A novel method called Acceptance Rejection Stitching has been devised for generating point process realizations, utilizing a combination of algorithms that can be accepted or rejected. This approach is particularly valuable when dealing with point processes for which precise algorithms may not be readily available. Using a point process commonly used in Bayesian analysis of Gaussian processes as a test case, simulations conducted via the proposed method demonstrated an ability to save substantial computational time by using a combination of more precise and faster algorithms. The generalization of this approach to higher dimensions is explored along with its application to multi-dimensional spatial processes.

In the context of Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP), we derive Galilean transformations modified by deformation, comparing them to the Lorentz transformations also obtained under GUP, which adhere to Einstein's principle of relativity. A simple momentum-based deformation leads to a set of Galilean transformations optimized by a specific function, enabling a unified approach to both special relativity and galilean mechanics within the GUP framework, resulting in deformed galilean symmetry groups, specifically the deformed galilean carbuncle symmetry group.

This research focuses on the resource allocation problem in multitasking systems, where the task of partitioning processing capacity among tasks is known as scheduling. Unlike previous studies on static resource partitioning, we explore the dynamic case and introduce two key contributions. Firstly, we introduce the Fractional Scheduling problem, where the processing capacity of a task is divided based on a fraction and can be used by other tasks in the background. A comprehensive investigation of this problem is conducted under various constraints, including off-line and on-line scenarios, with different task types and preemption rules. Secondly, the research extends to the on-line fractional scheduling problem with bounded task sizes, and a fractional algorithm is proposed that achieves a 2-approximation.

This study examines controlled hopping of a single rigid link supported by a single spring on a soft surface. The control is achieved through adjusting the spring force and the actuated joint's torque. The state feedback control strategy is designed using a quadratic programming approach, leveraging spring dynamics, and incorporates a projected feasible region based on the ground reaction force. The proposed control law is applied to a model of a human runner and, through numerical simulation, it is demonstrated that control can be effectively implemented even with imperfect ground and spring properties. The results also reveal that state feedback control provides improved trajectory tracking compared to open-loop actuation and has the added benefit of limiting impact forces on the ground, thus lowering the risk of injury.

This paper introduces a novel approach to rapidly and reliably update large-scale IoT networks by utilizing a High-Dimensional Random Walk strategy, compatible with standard IoT firmware update protocols. A new method, called Concurrent Transmission, is employed to transmit multiple pieces of firmware simultaneously to a subset of nodes in a large-scale IoT deployment. By optimizing speed and reliability in splitting and recombining data, this strategy overcomes the limitations of current methods in splitting and syncing updates. The proposed High-Dimensional Random Walk strategy utilizes a predefined set of locations, optimizing the transmission process to split into multiple subsets and move them to adjacent positions until all nodes have received the firmware update. A key advantage of this strategy is that it utilizes a small number of servers, and is applicable to various wireless network topologies, including mesh networks. The proposed approach has been tested in a real-world experiment involving a 100-node mesh network, demonstrating a 10-fold increase in transmission speed and 100% success rate in firmware updates.

A novel method, rooted in the concept of fractal dimensions, is used to identify critical characteristics of the transition in thermal states to many-body localization. The fractal dimensions linked to self-energy and eigenstates in both random ensemble averages and specific disorder configurations are used to map out key features of this phase transition. Notably, the self-energy dimensions show a distinct pattern, rising in the thermal phase before sharply shifting to a high value in the MBL state. Conversely, the eigenstate dimensions remain relatively stable in both MBL and thermal phases, only undergoing a phase shift in the thermodynamic limit. Furthermore, a correlation between the fractal dimensions of both MBL eigenstates and self-energy is established, along with an observation that the scaling behavior of self-energy dimensions in the thermal phase mirrors that of eigenstate dimensions.

This study presents the kBM-DP+ algorithm, a modified approach to address the complex problem of guiding multiple drones to a set of stationary targets with limited movement. Building upon a previously developed kBM-DP algorithm that initially solved this issue, kBM-DP+ enhances its performance by incorporating two key modifications to the original model. These changes significantly reduce the computational complexity and expand the algorithm's applicability to the more general problem of guiding drones under generalized dynamics.

Standard machine learning models, including binary and multi-class quantum classifiers built from unitary circuits with noise, are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks.  These attacks cause models to make incorrect or no predictions on deliberately altered input data, even with minimal changes.  In this research, we introduce a method for creating adversarial examples in the context of quantum data, and we verify that it results in vulnerable quantum neural networks.  Additionally, we propose an approach to enhance the robustness of these models.  Our method outperforms existing techniques in producing adversarial examples and demonstrates its applicability in the domain of quantum data.

In this research, our objective is to establish a precise upper limit on the volume-normalized l-th Steklov eigenvalue, denoted as $\lambda_l^{\Omega}(g)$, within a given domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, within a specified measure class $g$. This is achieved through the utilization of the Laplace transform and the Bochner-Dirichlet formula. Our findings reveal that in a spherical domain $B$ of a specific volume $V$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, our estimate aligns with the volume-normalized l-th Steklov eigenvalue of the domain $B$ when $l$ is a perfect square; otherwise, our estimate is found to be more conservative. Furthermore, our study explores the eigenvalue's continuity with respect to the domain's measure class when $l$ does not correspond to a perfect square.

Process mining has significantly contributed to process execution analysis through its ability to project process models from event logs via various trajectory-based alignments. Most existing techniques either convert techniques to traditional flow-based alignment or directly apply them to processes represented by transitions and activities. In contrast, to process simpler processes without cycles using event logs, a linear format using $\epsilon$ to denote no activity has been suggested. However, this method introduces unnecessary complexity. This research presents a novel method to align a simpler linear process with trajectories by transforming the process into a form suitable for standard zero-error alignment techniques.

This paper introduces a novel method to enhance the precision of radio propagation modeling by integrating deep convolutional neural networks (CNN) with conventional propagation models. A customized CNN architecture is designed, trained, and tested to accurately forecast signal strength. The approach leverages data from the Long-Term Evolution (LTE) network, enabling a comparison with both a standard method and a baseline CNN model. The study reveals that the personalization of the CNN architecture yields superior prediction results, showcasing the potential of deep learning techniques in radio propagation modeling and the importance of feature selection in this context.

This study explores the concept of integrating validation algorithms into temporal planning systems to enhance their problem-solving capabilities. By employing activity duration scaling, we demonstrate that such a valuation algorithm can be used to guide the temporal planner Focus, with the aim of accelerating solution discovery and elevating the solution quality. Furthermore, we introduce a family of accelerated valuation algorithms that enable the generation of high-quality plans in reduced time. These algorithms are combined with beam search to develop a family of search algorithms that outperform existing methods in generating near-optimal plans. Notably, these algorithms can be effectively applied to various optimization tasks beyond planning, such as solving Mixed Integer Linear Programming problems.

This research investigates the impact of allocating generation capacities out of balance with the grid network, a common practice in power system models. We compare two allocation methods using a model of California in 2020. The first approach applies a temporal filter to smooth out rapid changes in generation, while the second reallocates the additional generation during filtering to peak times. We find that ignoring out-of-balanced generation increases the costs of the power system by 1.5-2.5%, with a significant impact on the allocation of generation capacities, especially in models with a high level of temporal resolution. We recommend considering a simple method of balancing generation when analyzing policy and technology investments.

We analyze one-dimensional multi-component ionic Vlasov-Poisson models, which consist of Vlasov equations paired with either Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions for the Poisson equation. Due to a conserved quantity, these models possess equilibrium solutions, allowing us to prove the global existence of weak and weak-mild solutions, as well as the asymptotic stability of equilibrium solutions, with respect to the $L^1$ norm, under the assumption that the initial data has zero mean.

This paper outlines a search and rank approach that can effectively identify appropriate search terms for software change tasks, including those related to bug fixes and feature enhancements. As these two tasks rely heavily on the ability to locate relevant code, our method focuses on using task descriptions provided in these reports. It combines and optimizes two text mining techniques, TextRank and POSRank, which are applied to the full text of a task description to retain meaningful information. Additionally, for bug fix section descriptions, which are often limited, NFC is adapted to search the relevant function body, while also using language-specific tools to extract suitable search terms for other program features. Our experimental evaluation on 282 bug fix tasks and 108 bug or enhancement task demonstration sets from 8 projects demonstrated the effectiveness of our method, which is expected to be further validated through a controlled study on actual studies performed by 3 software engineers.

The behavior of ultrasound in various gels, known as rheo-acoustic gels, has been
studied and it's been found that the dynamics of the gel are influenced by its type.
Specifically, the movement of tiny particles within the gel when subjected to ultrasound
vary depending on the gel's composition. Moreover, the way in which the intensity of the
ultrasound correlates with the gel's movement differs significantly. Nevertheless,
when looking at certain scenarios, specifically low-frequency and low-intensity ultrasound,
it was discovered that the dynamics follow a consistent pattern across different types of the
gels. By creating computer models, researchers were able to study the movement within the gel
and they were able to explain why the dynamics have a consistent relationship with the intensity
of the ultrasound under these specific conditions.
The research demonstrates how the principles of mathematical induction can be applied to the Collatz conjecture.

The increasing adoption of machine learning and deep learning techniques has led to their application in various domains, including document classification. However, the complexity of these models often makes it difficult for users to comprehend the reasoning behind their predictions. To address this issue, the focus has shifted towards developing explainable AI methods, which can provide insights into the decision-making process of these models. This paper explores the concept of explainable AI in the context of document classification, highlighting the importance of understanding these models and the potential applications of AI explanations in the legal domain. To facilitate research in this area, the paper introduces a novel taxonomy for AI explanations and discusses the various types of explanations available, along with their associated methods. Furthermore, the paper identifies and analyzes several challenges that need to be addressed in order to improve explainability and trust in AI systems.

We have developed two novel concepts, individual and market utility, to investigate how public ratings affect agent preferences in large match markets. The utility of a matching for an agent is determined by its average rating among that agent's peers. We show that the utility function derived from stable ratings and preferences is well-defined, and that a stable ranking with large ratings also results in a stable match. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the market utility function is the limit of the average utility function as the market size becomes infinitely large, and that this average utility function is both well-defined and continuous. We also establish that the set of optimal matchings is non-empty, and that agent participation in the GS mechanism is incentivized for any market size. Furthermore, our research reveals that as market size grows, agents' utility functions become uncorrelated, and that a matching is optimal for an agent if and only if it is also optimal for her closest rivals.

Automated scoring of summary quality plays a vital role in evaluating the performance of summarization models. To enhance the accuracy of these scores, researchers have developed reference-free metrics, using perplexity and similarity to human judgments as guides. Building on this foundation, we introduce SummScore, a neural-based metric that leverages a contrastive loss to distinguish between good and bad summaries. In experiments, SummScore achieved a correlation with human scoring of 0.596 on the six datasets in the SummEval challenge, a significant improvement over the best existing metric (0.526). Furthermore, SummScore exhibits a higher correlation with human scoring than the state-of-the-art methods on six datasets, while also demonstrating a greater preference for diverse summaries.

Recovering the structure of signals from incomplete data is a common challenge in various fields, including astronomy, that often have to deal with signals heavily contaminated by interference. We developed an algorithm, Interstellar, to handle this problem, focusing on the interplay between cross-correlated data, data quality, and the ability to recover sparse structures. Through simulations, our study demonstrates that a significant portion of sparse structures can be recovered when using high-quality data, but this drops sharply as the data quality decreases. We found that when using high-quality data, noise levels can be reduced by a factor of 1000, but this benefit diminishes rapidly when using lower quality data. We found that when dealing with a range of substructures, our recovery rate drops dramatically, but this is not the case for more homogeneous structures. We used Interstellar to re-analyze a map of carbon monoxide emissions, and our study suggests that this map is contaminated by a web of structures that would have been missed by traditional imaging methods, but would have been identified by our algorithm.

This research introduces a novel, robust deep fusion architecture named BEVFusion that enables a robust combination of camera and LiDAR inputs for 3D object detection using representations within the bird's-eye-view feature space. The proposed framework leverages two-dimensional feature maps from bird's-eye-view (BEV) representations, derived from separate camera and LiDAR inputs, to accurately and efficiently predict object locations and rotation angles in the 3D space. By utilizing a novel cross-attention mechanism, the system seamlessly fuses information from both modalities. Furthermore, the framework's ability to perform robust object detection in the event of LiDAR sensor failures is demonstrated. Comprehensive evaluations conducted on the nuScenes and Waymo Open Dataset datasets confirm the superiority of our approach that outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of object detection accuracy.

The fluctuating hydrodynamics (FH) equation is a modification of the deterministic Navier-Stokes equation, incorporating a stochastic force. This addition is thought to cause the fluctuations that lead to the turbulence energy cascade and its dissipation. To investigate this, we apply a simple theory of turbulence, the eddy viscosity closure, to the FH equation and its deterministic counterpart. Our analysis shows that the stochastic force has no effect on the turbulence dissipation rate, thereby challenging a long-held assumption in turbulence research and casting doubt on the role of fluctuations in the turbulence energy cascade process.

We've conducted an experiment to study how a laser interacts with the surface of a heated fluid, resulting in striking diffraction patterns. As the surface ripples due to thermal changes, a beautiful diffraction grating emerges, causing a diffraction effect that appears to radiate outward from the liquid's surface in stunning patterns.

The design reuse repository known as Digital Design Mining (DDM) harnesses natural language processing to match design documentation and explore aggregated reuse collections. By adopting a model-agnostic strategy, DDM achieves adaptability across various design projects. Its two-pronged approach of conclusion stability enhancement and enhanced cross-domain applicability builds upon earlier design mining research. Building on this foundation, the study introduces a novel topic model that leverages documentation to uncover transferable design patterns and explores multiple text collections as a means to expand design reuse. Experimental findings validate the robustness of the approach, with two key innovations proposed: a conclusion stability technique that increases cross-project matching effectiveness, and a cross-project relevance increase through the integration of multiple text collections.

The proliferation of IoT devices has led to a significant increase in the amount of data generated, posing significant challenges in managing and processing this vast amount of data. To overcome these issues, a novel framework called H-STREAM has been developed to efficiently handle and process data streams from diverse IoT devices. By addressing the complexities associated with high-speed and high-volume data streams, H-STREAM effectively tackles these challenges. The framework features an advanced data storage system that allows for scalable and flexible access to data streams from heterogeneous sources. The efficacy of H-STREAM is demonstrated through its application in an urban air pollution monitoring system.

A novel, next-to-leading-order method for $V$-like quark ($Q'$) cross-section calculation in hadron collisions, where $Q'$ is produced in pairs, is presented. The approach leverages the resonance approximation, which accurately captures the dominant resonant diagrams, and the non-resonant terms, estimated through analytical wide resonance models. The method's cross-section estimates for Q' masses ranging from 800 to 1200 GeV are found to be accurate, with errors of 10% or less for Q' masses of 800, 900, and 1000 GeV. The study also outlines the implementation of the code in FORTRAN.

This research introduces the first application of sequence-to-sequence techniques for generating SPARQL queries. A tailored encoder-decoder model is developed, utilizing a graph-based encoder to represent SPARQL query structure and an attention mechanism to link generated tokens with the graph. A substantial dataset of 200,000 pairs of complex queries and text descriptions is leveraged for training. We demonstrate that the proposed decoder can be integrated with existing text2sparQL systems to enhance their capabilities for handling intricate queries. Additionally, we present a new dataset consisting of 100 graph concepts and evaluate our approach on both fresh and dataset-based datasets.

Our research centers on the temporal evolution of specific research domains within the venue publishing community, spanning across various venues and over extended periods. By applying a data-driven methodology, we have derived key insights into the shifting interests and focal points in Computer Science over the past 30 years. This study reveals the interconnectedness of sub-disciplines and how the migration of research within distinct venues has significantly impacted the redistribution of publishing activity. By providing a comprehensive and granular view of the evolution of individual research fields, we aim to facilitate a deeper comprehension of the intricate dynamics governing the evolution of the scientific knowledge base.

This research aims to leverage the advancements in computer vision and machine learning to improve robustness verification of neural networks applied to control systems. Building on converging developments in these areas, we propose a novel approach to expedite the development of scalable and efficient verification tools. Moreover, this work marks a significant step in the intersection of control theory and neural networks by introducing a bridge between the advancements in deep learning, computer vision, and machine learning communities and robustness verification of neural networks for control systems.

Functorial clustering schemes are utilized in both mathematics and computer science to tackle key challenges in clustering tasks. However, they are plagued by a significant drawback: the inability to handle non-ultrametric data effectively. To rectify this limitation, we introduce an extended version of functorial schemes that can handle the broader class of data sets, thus fully capturing diverse clustering methods employed in various fields. These enhancements include flexible choices of metric, limit type, and direction of limits. Furthermore, we explore several applications of these improved functorial schemes, including hierarchical clustering and k-means clustering.

In various applications such as surveillance, virtual production, and augmented reality, completing the streaming data from cameras with unknown perspectives is crucial. Existing methods, which rely on the relationship between tensor components, struggle in scenes with motion due to increased prediction errors. This paper introduces an efficient, real-time solution for filling in the gaps of dynamic videos from obscured areas, leveraging a neural network. A key innovation is establishing a connection between tensor completion and image inpainting, allowing the network to handle both static and moving scenes. Additionally, we develop a dynamic version of Ne4Tensor, a previous method, which significantly improves text handling in moving scenes. Our approach outperforms real-time inpainting techniques and excels over prior tensor completion methods in moving environments, as shown by experimental results.

This study categorizes certain Weyl group Nichols algebras into finite-dimensional cases. The analysis focuses on classical Weyl groups with specific tube classifications and demonstrates that associated Nichols algebras are finite in dimension if the braiding has a quantum defect. We further confirm the finite-dimensional nature of certain pre-Lie algebras by identifying specific subalgebras within the Weyl group algebras.

Researchers investigated the development of inertial wave turbulence in zero viscosity, incompressible flows within rapidly rotating bounded environments. Utilizing an exact inertial wave spectrum derived by G. I. Taylor in 1955, they successfully verified the Coriolis-type $N^2k_v^{-5/3}$ spectrum, observed in experiments, through numerical simulations. The results revealed that the Taylor spectrum remains consistent with Kolmogorov's energy spectrum, confirming that inertial wave turbulence transports energy at the inertial frequency corresponding to the inverse of the forcing timescale.

We present an iterative graph normalization technique, the applications of which
extend beyond estimating the size of the Maximum Weight Independent Set and include
the optimization of other subgraph-induced weighted parameters. Notably, the
approach is also a practical method for quickly eliminating vertices that are not
part of any Maximum Weight Independent Set. Furthermore, the technique is a step
in a weighted version of the inverse of the Motif Finding problem. The
normalization process is a weighted variant of a known Vizing algorithm for
coloring graphs. The quick independent set estimation method is based on a proof
of a long-standing Vazirani conjecture, the quick independent set proof being a
step towards a broader long-standing Vizing conjecture. The fast independent set
estimation method is a component of a broader algorithm for the weighted
Maximum Weight Independent Set problem, the algorithm also being able to handle
the optimization of other subgraph-induced weighted parameters. The algorithm is
a step towards a solution of a more general problem, the existence of a
polynomial-time approximation scheme for Maximum Weight Independent Set. The
approach is also a step towards the identification of the Minimum Dominating Set.

This research explores the Landau Level Oscillations of a two-dimensional Dirac Fermi system in a Landau, in the presence of electric modulation and a magnetic field oriented perpendicularly.  We have observed Landau Level Oscillations of the system's energy in both even and odd Landau Levels.  By adjusting the electric modulation, a complete suppression of the even Landau Levels was observed.  Furthermore, a suppression of the odd Landau Levels is also evident.  A calculated density of states for the system is presented, demonstrating a significant dependence on the Landau Levels' symmetry.  A phase diagram for the system is also proposed.  Our research has also found Shubnikov de Haas Oscillations in the system's resistance, in addition to demonstrating Landau Level Oscillations in the system's energy.  A comparison of the measured and calculated values of the carrier density reveals a significant agreement.  A unique aspect of our research is the observation of Shubnikov de Haas Oscillations in the system's even and odd Landau Levels.  A unique feature of our research is the observation of Shubnikov de Haas Oscillations in the system's even and odd Landau Levels.

We conducted a radio observation of the M dwarf binary, CR Draconis, at 3.6 GHz using the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope. Our measurements revealed that the emission from this M dwarf was approximately 100 times stronger than Jupiter's, characterized by structure similar to that of the planet and highly polarized similar to Jupiter. In contrast to the Sun, the emission was not continuum but rather bursty, with some bursts coinciding with optical flares, while others did not. Moreover, the polarization of these bursts was consistent with that of the continuum, indicating a common emission origin. Our findings suggest that the emission from the M dwarf was likely generated by the interaction between its hot coronal wind and the orbiting planets, rather than by traditional star-planet interaction mechanisms. This research provides the first direct evidence that hot coronal winds from M dwarfs can produce detectable radio emission and potentially significant activity from hot coronae in multi-planet systems.

To fully utilize neural rendering techniques, it's crucial to develop a framework that can handle multiple, moving objects. A new approach, called Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR), is presented, which overcomes previous limitations by supporting multiple, dynamic objects. ANR achieves this through the use of a hierarchical framework, which combines multiple surjective neural fields (NFSs) to accurately model complex scenes. In this method, each NFS handles a specific part of the scene, allowing the system to scale effectively even when dealing with large objects and multiple moving parts. ANR is tested and validated through various experiments, including those involving a robotic arm and other complex scenes, which demonstrate its ability to accurately reproduce detailed textures and structures. These results show that ANR outperforms previous methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

Human visual systems are capable of identifying objects despite significant image distortions, but current artificial neural networks often struggle with similar tasks. To circumvent this limitation, researchers have developed specialized architectures, like the multilevel invariant network (MIN), to teach artificial networks to disregard distorted features. However, this approach has a drawback of requiring significant time and resources. To address this, researchers have proposed the cooperative multilevel invariant network (CMIN), which incorporates a novel self-organizing map (SOM) layer to accelerate learning and reduce the need for hyperparameter adjustments. By employing cross-domain evaluations, these researchers have demonstrated that CMIN outperforms traditional deep networks and other state-of-the-art architectures in recognizing objects across various contexts and even surpasses the human visual system in certain tasks.

Chains of Wilson loops in 3d Chern-Simons theory with compact gauge groups exhibit closed algebraic relations. Specifically, the expectation values of Wilson loops following conjugacy classes in a linear setup satisfy closed algebraic relations. These relationships define representations of the Askey-Wilson algebra, which include quadratic q-deformed SU(2) and su(2)_2 spin chains. By using large q expansions of SU(2) Wilson loops, the validity of the AW algebra's closure is demonstrated without requiring the quantum group structure. This phenomenon is also seen in 3d Chern-Simons theories with non-compact gauge groups.

The sign problem in bosonic superfluids is addressed by employing a novel basis in quantum Monte Carlo simulations. This basis, comprising atomic wave functions grouped into trimers, represents the wave function of $N$ atoms as a product of $N/2$ basis functions, paired with the remaining unpaired basis if $N$ is odd. When applied to low-temperature simulations of the Bose-Hubbard model, the trimers-based approach significantly enhances the sign problem, reducing the relative variance of the measurement by the relative variance of the sign, yielding a variance/sign ratio as low as $0.01$. This improvement outperforms conventional methods, with the sign ratio/superfluid fraction ratio being $10^{-4}$, based on statistical noise of $10^{-6}$. This work represents a groundbreaking approach to representing interacting bosonic systems with periodic boundary conditions, providing substantial computational savings for simulations of low-temperature quantum phenomena.

This study aims to assess the capabilities of state-of-the-art language models in identifying unseen emotions and cognitive traits. We investigate how the size of the model, its training objectives, and its starting point influence its performance. We discovered that larger models tend to achieve better results, while varying training objectives led to diverse outcomes. Notably, we observed that pre-trained models already contain a wealth of knowledge about emotions and cognitive traits, which enables them to excel in certain tasks even without any fine-tuning.

In this research, we use CosmoTransitions to investigate in detail a detailed search for a parameter space region within the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model that could potentially be favored by recent Strong First Order Phase Transition evidence from Strong First Order Phase Transition evidence from recent LHC analysis. An extensive examination of this region is conducted, focusing on the model's predicted properties of the Higgs boson, the thermal relic density of dark matter particles, and the STRP effect. Our analysis of the STRP effect is the most thorough to date within this framework, and our results are then compared with current experimental data from the Large Hadron Collider, the Planck satellite, and direct detection experiments. Our research demonstrates that no areas within this framework are compatible with both the observational evidence from the Planck satellite, current experimental data from the Large Hadron Collider, and the predicted STRP effect.

The rapid pace of research on the intergalactic medium (IGM) has been fueled by observations of distant radio galaxies, which have provided valuable insights into the properties of the IGM. Although deep continuum observations have been successful in identifying redshifts for galaxies at z = 2 - 4, such evidence is still limited. We conducted a study of a radio galaxy at z = 4.015 using the Atacama Large Millimetre/submillimetre Array (ALMA) to determine its robust redshift. We also used ALMA to measure the rest-frame optical flux of the galaxy, which was found to be consistent with predictions from a standard Eddington-limited model. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the galaxy's black hole mass is estimated to be approximately 1.5 x 10^9 solar masses. We have developed a method for using the ALMA to identify and characterize the properties of distant radio galaxies, which can be used to establish a correlation between the growth of supermassive black holes and the properties of their host galaxies.

We've established a correlation between low-lying excitations of monopoless and Dirac spin liquid phases using a model based on the interplay of spin and charge degrees of freedom. This model, featuring an emergent $U(1)$ gauge field, reveals that the spin liquid phase is associated with charged spinons, neutral monopoles, and a dynamic gauge field. A key indicator of Dirac spin liquid is the presence of a finite gap in the monopole spectrum. However, our findings show a distinct relationship between low-lying monopole excitations and certain spin liquid phases, specifically N\'eel-doped spin liquids with neutral spinons. In the case of these N\'eel-doped spin liquids, a finite density of monopoles is introduced, resulting in the softening of the monopole excitations. This discovery provides a novel method for identifying spin liquid phases in condensed matter systems through the observation of low-lying monopole excitations.

The work of Di Francesco, Jotzu, and Leroux on a lattice system with spontaneously broken $Z_3$ symmetry has been analyzed and extended using the three-state Potts model. It is found that the symmetry breaking caused by temporal lattice size increases and is also influenced by a control parameter. As the imaginary time extends, the breaking strength grows, and the phase boundary separating the ordered and disordered states can be mapped out. Introducing a parameter that manages noise levels allows the investigation of how this factor impacts symmetry breaking. Furthermore, the amount of symmetry breaking at a specific control parameter can be measured, and the findings are also valid for a related discrete system.

A novel Cr$_2$Al compound, which shares structural similarities with non-reciprocal topological insulator Mn$_2$Au, has been discovered. High-precision synchrotron X-ray diffraction and first-principles calculations confirm that Cr$_2$Al exhibits a non-centrosymmetric, orthorhombic Pnma structure, with a body-centered arrangement, and exhibits unique magnetic characteristics. The magnetic ordering of Cr atoms in the compound is characterized by ferromagnetic connections along the c-axis, but antiferromagnetic connections along the a- and b-axes, differing significantly from the antiferromagnetic connections along the c-axis, but ferromagnetic connections along the a- and b-axes, as observed in Mn$_2$Au. The unique magnetic structure allows for the potential occurrence of magnetic-related phenomena, such as the magnetic Hall effect, in Cr$_2$Al.

In the study of rarefied microflows, thermal transpiration is an important phenomenon. To investigate this phenomenon, we compare the predictions of two kinetic models, one based on hard-sphere molecules and the other accounting for real molecule effects. These models are implemented using the slip-flow, transition, and free-molecular flow regimes. The results show that the transition regime is not accurately captured by either model, but the model based on $u$-behavior of cross sections, or $u$-model, shows better agreement with direct simulation Monte Carlo method or DSMC simulation data. This $u$-model is therefore a more reliable tool for simulating thermal transpiration in rarefied microflows.

This paper presents a novel approach to few-shot semantic parsing that leverages
large language models (LLMs) and incorporates unsupervised data, such as image
captions, to create a more robust training set. The proposed framework utilizes
the captioned images as prompts to generate semantic parses through a guided process
that enables the model to identify the correct output. Furthermore, it integrates a
contrastive loss to refine the predictions and enhance the model's performance.
Evaluations on the Visual2SQL task demonstrate that this method outperforms state-of
the-art techniques in terms of few-shot settings and matches zero-shot performance.

High-energy particle physics experiments, such as the Large Hadron Collider, utilize specific tracking detectors to accurately measure charged particles. The experiments' demands require updates to particle physics sensors, and certain technologies developed for next-gen experiments like the FCC-ee and FCC-hh are expected to significantly reduce radiation damage over decades of operation. This study evaluates two specific sensor technologies using specialized variants, the Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor and Low Gain Avalanche Diode, which have shown exceptional performance in previous experiments. Utilizing a high-intensity proton beam at the CERN Irradiation Facility, these specialized variants were tested under various radiation doses up to 10 Mrad, exceeding the LHC's design radiation limit by an order of magnitude, to assess their performance. Comprehensive electrical and geometric measurements were conducted to assess the sensors' resilience, and their performance under increased radiation doses exceeded expectations.

The X-ray low-mass AGN 2XMM J123103.2+110648 has been observed by the eROSITA telescope in a high-resolution mode. The AGN's X-ray emission was detected to have significant variability, with the 2021-09-08 observation revealing an almost tenfold increase in brightness compared to the 2019-07-18 event. The AGN's X-ray spectrum displayed a complex shape, with the emission rate fluctuating between 0.1-10 keV ranges and 100-100000 keV ranges in a manner suggesting a relationship between flux and temperature. The X-ray emission rate of 2021-09-08 was analyzed in relation to the black hole's mass, resulting in a 0.000001% - 0.001% luminosity-to-Eddington ratio, with the energy range of 0.1-10 keV. The X-ray emission rate of 2021-09-08 was also analyzed in a 100-100000 keV energy range, with the emission rate being 0.000001% - 0.001% with a gamma-ray spectrum slope of -1.19. The X-ray emission

We've conducted a groundbreaking study of B types magnetic stars, including 10 new discoveries, by examining their surrounding environments. Our analysis of 149 B types magnetic stars across the entire sky has revealed that these stars have a significantly lower rate of X-ray emission than expected, based on our comprehensive 200-3000\AA band photometric observations. This has led to the identification of two distinct groups of B types magnetic stars, with one group showing a strong correlation between X-ray emission and the rotational velocity of the star's magnetic field. Our findings indicate that these B types magnetic stars have magnetospheres formed from the surrounding circumstellar disk material, with a distinct separation between non-magnetic and magnetically isolated stars. This has far-reaching implications for our understanding of planetary formation, as well as the evolution of binary systems and the distribution of exoplanets.

The connection to generalized orthogonal polynomials is established by operators that fit into specific relationships. Consider the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator's creation and annihilation operators D+, D-. The specific differential operators E and Ej, related to generalized Hermite and Gegenbauer polynomials, serve as intertwining operators between certain representations of SU(1,1) and U(1,1). A generalized polynomial operator j0 is presented, enabling a direct mapping between U(1,1) and SU(1,1) representations and facilitating the construction of correlated generalized orthogonal polynomials for SU(1,1) and SU(3) representations.

We have conducted an in-depth analysis of the relationship between star formation rates measured through H30α and infrared fluxes for 15 nearby galaxies with low metallicity. Our research indicates that comparing these two measurements can result in infrared star formation rates significantly higher (up to 5 times) than those based on H30α. This discrepancy primarily arises from the fact that older star populations, which are more prominent in low-metallicity environments, contribute to the infrared radiation but not the H30α emission. Our findings suggest that inferring stellar properties from low-metallicity galaxies may lead to an overestimation of their star formation rates if based solely on infrared data without considering the age of the star population. This has significant implications for the interpretation of low-metallicity galaxies observed with local probes, as well as the modeling of high-redshift galaxies, where the age of star populations and metallicity are often poorly understood.

There are two distinct types of continuous, minimal actions that can occur on spaces with totally disconnected topology. These involve the use of virtually cyclic groups and the infinite dihedral group. Our key finding reveals a fundamental difference between these group types, based on the underlying topological space's structure. Specifically, we establish that there is a continuous, minimal action involving the dihedral group on a specific, non-trivial topology, but no such virtually cyclic group can replicate this same topology. Our research also builds on established theories, such as Ellis' theorem and Milnor's work, to establish a deeper understanding of these group types and their underlying topological properties.

A general method for finding a low-dimensional subspace to approximate complex functions is presented in this dissertation. To achieve this, novel techniques combining non-asymptotic methods and reproducing kernel kernels are developed. As a result, the proposed techniques offer significant advantages over traditional projection methods in terms of efficiency and accuracy. Furthermore, several practical applications of the proposed framework are demonstrated through numerical experiments, highlighting its versatility in handling key tasks such as feature selection and dimensionality reduction.

This work presents a computational framework for estimating the state of complex systems, using the example of an epidemic model. We introduce a novel observer structure, based on the Extended Kalman Filter, that effectively handles non-linear systems. By integrating local linear models, our architecture enables efficient state estimation. We evaluate the efficacy of our framework in real-time on heterogeneous hardware, demonstrating a significant improvement in performance through parallel processing. Furthermore, the addition of noise removal techniques and estimation of initial conditions further enhances the accuracy of our method.

Enhancing temporal knowledge graph embeddings is crucial for capturing changing dynamics within temporal knowledge graphs. However, the lack of a comprehensive benchmark hinders comparative evaluations of proposed methods. In response, we introduce NKPT, a novel embedding model that leverages PageCurve to capture temporal profiles and incorporates time complexity concepts. Our comparative study of NKPT with five existing methods reveals that it consistently outperforms them across multiple evaluation metrics, particularly for entities. Moreover, NKPT excels in tasks requiring temporal reasoning and is highly effective in predicting both entities and time frames. Our proposed method and extensive benchmarking data are publicly available on GitHub.

For Kerr-lens mode-locking to stabilize, a finely-tuned balance of nonlinearity, lensing, and aperture size is required.  However, the single-pass nonlinearity in typical Ti:Sa lasers is insufficient, and most mode-locking stability is attributed to the dynamic nonlinearity from amplitude fluctuations.  Our research focuses on the electro-optic modulator, a passive element that can stabilize Kerr-lens mode-locked lasers by addressing phase fluctuations.  The EOM is modeled and its impact on KLML stability is studied through simulations, revealing substantial improvements in stability, reduced pulse energy, and lower threshold requirements.  The EOM's efficacy is further demonstrated experimentally in a Ti:Sa laser, achieving significant enhancements in KLML stability, substantial reductions in the threshold, and shorter turn-up times in relation to conventional systems.

In the realm of machine learning, Federated Learning has garnered significant attention as a decentralized training technique, where multiple devices collaborate to train a model while safeguarding user data privacy. A crucial aspect of FL involves data exchange between participants, and this study focuses on optimizing data exchange in asynchronous ASYNC-FED. First, a novel paradigm called Partial-Sharing-Based Communication (PSBC) is introduced, which allows for a reduction in communication costs for participants. Next, a multi-objective optimization problem is formulated to achieve the best communication efficiency and model performance, followed by an efficient solution approach. Finally, the proposed method is validated through experiments, demonstrating its superiority over existing communication protocols across various dimensions.

Optical absorption in thin silicon films is significantly enhanced by employing a photonic crystal back reflector, allowing for efficient absorption even with very thin films. Experimental results show that a 100 nm thick silicon film with a second-order photonic crystal back reflector can achieve an absorption rate of 90% at 1550 nm. Furthermore, the absorption peak in the second spectral order exhibits a strong dependence on the silicon film's thickness, with a rate of 2.8% per nm.

Two specific functions, related to the exponential map's dynamics in the complex plane, are the focus of this paper. These relations, $\rho_1(\xi)$ and \rho_2(\xi)$, are defined as the unique solutions to specific equations. These unique solutions exist within specific domains and take specific values on their respective boundaries. These unique solutions play a significant role in parameterizing certain regions and dynamic phenomena associated with the exponential map, including Siegel disks and parabolic basins. Additionally, the paper explores specific growth properties of these functions, their relationship to other known functions, and the derivation of precise estimates for their moduli, which can be visualized within specific regions and dynamic phenomena associated with the exponential map.

We suggest a theoretical framework based on high-dimensional expanders that could lead to the creation of new explicit constructions and potentially establish a source for deterministic generators, although this remains unproven. These expanders may be useful in various fields of theoretical computer science, including algorithm design and data structure development, and we discuss a few possible applications.

The coexistence of a non-magnetic quantum spin liquid (QSL) and a recently discovered quantum spin-adjacency (QSQA) state is observed in Gd$^{3+}$ ions arranged in a geometrically frustrated pyrochlore lattice within the compound GdInO$_3$. Utilizing inelastic neutron scattering, researchers have discovered that the dynamic spin correlations within gapped levels exhibit characteristics of a QSL state that persists across the entire magnetic zone. The data also indicates that these gapped levels show signs of QSQA, specifically exhibiting enhanced intensity along the directions parallel and perpendicular to the Gd ions. Furthermore, researchers have identified a correlated structure in the QSL state where there is increased intensity along the directions defined by the Gd bonds. The findings provide a rare experimental example of QSQA within a QSL state, and the study offers insights into the quantum entanglement between spins and gapped excitations.

In various real-world applications, such as social network analysis and machine learning, it's crucial to extract meaningful information from network nodes.  A key factor in determining the importance of nodes in graph-based networks is their connections to other nodes.  In this paper, a new approach is presented for representing nodes in graphs, which involves calculating the sum of normalized adjacency matrices up to a certain order, while also considering the maximum distance between connected nodes.  To address the issue of high computational complexity, an iterative algorithm is proposed for calculating these representations.  Furthermore, the representation is refined by discarding less significant connections to the nodes, resulting in more compact graphs.  A theoretical analysis demonstrates that these refined graphs accurately capture the essential characteristics of the original graphs.  The effectiveness of this approach is validated through experiments on graph classification and semi-supervised learning, where it is shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance.

A value-added pill, which serves as a heat and humidity source, undergoes a rapid activation process upon exposure to high temperatures. This process involves transitioning from a solid state to a gas state, facilitated by a heating element that elevates the pill's temperature above its sublimation point. A two-compartment system, which places the pill in a separate chamber from the heating element, offers advantages in vapor generation due to reduced congestion in the vapor-producing volume. A computational model, which simulates the process using the finite volume method, accurately captures the phase transition and heat transfer dynamics. By incorporating the experimentally determined sublimation enthalpy and heat of fusion, the model demonstrates satisfactory agreement with measured temperature and mass loss data. Furthermore, the model predicts the growth of the gas phase and subsequent cooling of the liquid phase, which, when combined with a suitable temperature, yields optimal vapor rates. This mechanism, which utilizes a gas-permeable membrane separating the two chambers, has significant implications for the design of systems that utilize the pill's vapor for cooling and humidity control.

This research explores polarisation-multiplexed formats, widely employed in high-capacity optical communications, by introducing novel, non-linear interference models. These models are based on a geometric framework that is both mathematically precise and computationally efficient. They are formulated in place-based and path-based models, which are then compared to a standard approximation via simulations. The path-based model is further applied to study the dynamics of optical phase conjugation in a dual-channel system.

Recent advancements in deep learning (DL) for image fusion have yielded impressive results. However, when applied to fire imagery, fusing images with high noise levels and blurred features often leads to the propagation of false positives. Notably, both traditional methods and DL-based approaches exhibit a significant rate of false positives, which can hinder their effectiveness. To address this issue, this study presents a novel approach that selectively eliminates false positives by leveraging the characteristics of fire and the inherent structure of the input images. The proposed method, referred to as fire fusion with structural prior, utilizes a neural network to generate a structural prior from the input images, which is then used to guide the fusion process. By doing so, the false positives in the fused image are significantly reduced, as evidenced by the substantial improvements in objective metrics, such as SNR, and subjective evaluations. The source code is available on GitHub for further reference.

Diagnosing mental health conditions on social media presents a more nuanced challenge than it might seem. While social media data can be used to identify mental health issues, it's not as accurate as physical examinations due to the informal and sometimes inaccurate nature of online communications. Researchers have developed a machine learning model that leverages social media data to predict depression and anxiety in users. This model employs information from social media profiles to improve its predictions, outperforming the state-of-the-art in multiple testing scenarios. Despite its success, the issue of data sparsity remains a significant concern, with some social media datasets containing a significant percentage of missing data. To address this challenge, a novel approach called GraphFusion is proposed, which combines information from online sources and integrates it into a unified graph representation. This graph is then used to predict mental health issues, significantly improving the accuracy of predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that GraphFusion outperforms the state-of-the-art in multiple tests, even on sparse data, and also disprove the common notion that social media data is redundant, rather than complementary, to other forms of data.

This research introduces a novel two-level decision-making process to tackle the management of SARS-CoV-2 outbreaks. We model hospital and healthcare institution staff as decision-makers capable of making supply chain decisions, such as administering vaccines and treatments, which can be viewed as a Stackelberg game, where the leader's actions affect the follower's behavior. Meanwhile, government authorities implement restrictive measures, such as curfews, to contain the coronavirus. We analyze how hospital and government actions impact the RS epidemic using numerical simulations, revealing the effectiveness of hospital interventions in combination with government controls. We also propose the development of optimal hospitals and government supply chains to contain the pandemic.

The interaction between two specific nuclear resonances, namely the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance and the Isoscalar Giant Quadrupole Resonance, impacts their energy structure. This interaction is analyzed using a mathematical model that simulates their coupling. Furthermore, the isoscalar giant multipole resonances' behavior with deformation is also studied using the same model.

This research explores the impact of region-specific friction thresholds on feedback loop motion in oscillating systems, using a mass-spring system as a model. When the feedback gain is high, the mass exhibits chaotic motion in the absence of friction. However, introducing the stiction interval introduces intervals of rest, allowing for the creation of a Poincaré map that reveals specific conditions required for rest periods to occur and understand the dynamics of resting solutions. Furthermore, researchers established limits on the size of the stiction interval that guarantee the development of a resting limit cycle, which becomes a globally attracting solution under a spring-like restoring force. In contrast, the dynamics become more complex with non-linear or non-linear restoring forces and no general criteria currently exist to determine the possibility of a resting limit cycle in the p-stable case.

The effectiveness of various trading strategies has been analyzed in relation to market frictions, such as transaction costs and liquidity issues. A numerical model of a market is created to examine the impact of trading costs and limits on two trading strategies: a mean-reverting strategy and a momentum-based strategy. The analysis reveals the distinct effects of market frictions on each strategy's performance.

In recent years, the field of recommender systems has gained significant attention, 
driven by the need to enhance user experience and reduce information overload. 
However, the dynamic nature of user preferences poses a challenge, 
resulting in inaccurate recommendations and a suboptimal experience. 
To address this issue, it is crucial to comprehend user intent and tailor the 
recommendation strategy accordingly. 
This paper introduces an innovative framework that leverages both explicit and 
implicit user interactions to create a comprehensive user intent profile. 
By integrating the user's explicit actions, such as ratings, and implicit behaviors, 
like implicit feedback, it is possible to obtain a nuanced understanding of user 
intent. 
Building upon this intent profile, it is possible to develop a more accurate user 
model that accurately captures user preferences. 
This model is then utilized to recommend items that best suit the user's intent. 
Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance 
of our approach compared to state-of-the-art methods.

In this analysis, a reducible variation of the confluent Heun equation is
investigated with parameters $(b, a_1, A, B)$. A solution to this equation is
derived and, under the condition that $b$ is a non-zero integer and the sum
of the other parameters is a non-zero integer, the existence of a valid
equation is established. Given this condition, the reducible equation yields a
holomorphic solution across the entire complex plane with the exception of the
origin, and we, therefore, determine the series expansion of this solution.

Low-rank matrix recovery is a common challenge in many scientific disciplines, including astronomy, where researchers often encounter issues with the recovery of signals from noisy, incomplete data. Principal component analysis (PCA) is a standard method for this recovery, particularly useful in scenarios where the matrix elements are weighted combinations of data, such as astronomical images. However, it's been observed that PCA can yield less accurate results for such weighted combinations, prompting an investigation into why this occurs and how to resolve it. This study demonstrates that PCA's limitations stem from a fundamental assumption about the relationship between the matrix weights and the data. By redefining this relationship, equivalent to applying a pre-processing procedure, we can achieve better recovery results. This equivalence reveals that PCA's limitations are not inherent, but can be overcome through this pre-processing step.

The presence of fractional boundary states in quantum systems with non-integer spin is well-documented, but it is unclear how these states are represented in classical systems or systems without spin symmetry. We have discovered a new mechanism to generate fractional boundary states in classical systems by exploiting interactions between distinct fractional modes of the same symmetry class, for instance, combining states with spin up and down to form a classical spin-0 system exhibiting topological properties. This phenomenon can be observed in various physical systems, such as electronic circuits with non-reciprocal interactions and ultracold atoms in Raman setups, providing potential avenues for its experimental verification.

We have developed a novel approach to enhance the sensitivity of the LHCb detector in detecting transitions of b to s l+ l- by exploiting additional decay pathways for the B meson and a tight spatial correlation between the b and lepton particles. Since the variant using B meson decay products shows comparable performance to tracking muons from the decay of tau particles, it may be particularly advantageous for studies on b to s mu+ mu- transitions and other related processes.

In networked systems, ensuring the stability of individual or multiple controllers is a major challenge. A proposed method involves adapting a well-known algorithm, originally developed for single-hop networks, to multi-hop networks. By incorporating algorithmic features into the controller, it becomes resilient to network disruptions and even adaptive for systems with time-varying parameters. A specific implementation of this concept is demonstrated using a two-node example with algorithm parameter tuning, effectively stabilizing a system with changes in Bass's algorithm. Furthermore, the approach is applied to two real-world systems: a two-reactor chemical system and a two-area power network, both exhibiting time-varying characteristics.

Our proposed framework efficiently identifies low-deceleration events in free-flow traffic using E-NOISE, detecting drops in speed greater than 10 km/h. It combines three components: an automated loop for E-NOISE feature extraction, a universal clustering method to create feature subsets, and a feature selection process to optimize classification accuracy. Our framework achieved state-of-the-art performance, with 97.1% accuracy on the validation dataset and 98.1% precision. Notably, it outperformed existing models by reducing total error rate and false negative rate while maintaining a comparable true alert rate and false alert rate.

This code is a versatile analytical toolbox for complex network studies and comprehensive data visualization. The code initially leverages data from specific experiments or simulations, executes various network stability and synchronization analyses using established analytical approaches, and generates an in-depth understanding of the results. Following the analytical process, the code produces detailed visualizations of the network along with associated data like node positions, node properties, coupling, and time series. These visualizations are easily customizable to accommodate individual research requirements.

Evolutionary and ecological interactions share similarities in their reliance on resource-based feedback loops, yet traditional evolutionary theory relies on distinct mathematical frameworks from ecological models due to historical development. To address this, researchers have developed a unified model that can be analyzed using established ecological principles, taking into account the fundamental role of temperature and genetic variability in influencing the speed and stability of evolutionary and ecological dynamics. A combined analysis reveals the existence of co-evolutionary stability, which can be further explored through numerical simulations and may have significant implications for understanding long-term evolutionary outcomes, potentially leading to insights about ecological relationships within populations.

Recent studies have exposed the susceptibility of speech representation models to attacks by a knowledgeable adversary. In the case of the x-vector model, this means the attacker can manipulate input audio to make the model misidentify speakers. In our research, we examine how x-vectors respond to two types of audio manipulation: speaker swapping and voice conversion. Our findings reveal that x-vectors are easily influenced by both methods when the attacker has full knowledge. However, when the attacker has limited knowledge, the impact is significantly reduced, with manipulation being 10 times less effective in the speaking style attack compared to the speaker swapping attack.

Automated Market Makers in liquidity pools can be exploited by arbitrageurs, causing the order book's pricing curve to become skewed and less efficient. The degree of distortion is determined by the arbitrageurs' activity levels, which is a concept known as "mining." In this context, we investigate the effects of the mining parameter on the order book, focusing on the curvature of the pricing curve in Constant Product Automated Market Makers. We find that the price for high-demand assets is generally higher, but lower prices for low-demand assets may lead to reduced investor gains. In an experiment with risk-averse Automated Market Makers, we discovered that the pricing curve can be inverted, with high-demand assets priced lower than low-demand assets. We also analyze the impact of this distortion on the potential for arbitrage and the potential earnings of liquidity providers. Furthermore, we consider the effects of multiple assets in Automated Market Makers and the potential for more complex pricing models to emerge.

This research develops an entropy-based stability measure, referred to as an E-value, to assess the reliability of causal inferences in an orienting framework that utilizes sensitivity analysis to account for unmeasured confounding when data is missing. Building on previous work that explored the sample entropy of causal graphs, we investigate the sample entropy of a specific class of sensitivity bounds and establish an E-value that quantifies the robustness of causal inferences in the presence of missing data. A key contribution of our study is the demonstration of the E-value's applicability to univariate sensitivity bounds, such as those introduced by VanderWeele and others, and we further examine its extended use with multi-dimensional sensitivity bounds. A practical example demonstrates how our method can assess the robustness of conclusions regarding individual and joint treatment effects.

Certain free actions of the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ on the quantum plane, which are also known as quantum planes, are explored. These actions can be grouped based on two distinct classes. The two groups of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ are not related and each has specific properties that distinguish them. The work provides an explicit classification of the distinct classes of the planes under consideration. The study also connects to noncommutative tori, which are similar concepts in the field.

The Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has become a crucial component in modern society, with vehicles generating and exchanging vast amounts of sensitive data. This has raised significant concerns regarding data security and privacy, prompting the need for an effective security framework. This paper assesses the potential of applying Blockchain technology to IoVs applications, focusing on its key features that contribute to secure data handling, such as decentralization, distributed ledgers, and smart contracts. Furthermore, we explore the integration of Blockchain with other emerging technologies, such as cloud computing, edge computing, and blockchain oracles, to enhance IoVs functionality. Lastly, this paper identifies the challenges associated with Blockchain implementation in IoVs and proposes future research directions to address these issues.

Measurements of the fragmentation fraction of heavy quarks into the $B^0_s$ meson, denoted as $f_{B^0_s}$, are conducted using data collected from $pp$ collisions at 7 and 8 TeV by the LHCb detector. This study utilizes the semileptonic decay modes of $B^0_s$ and employs the ratio of observed to expected yields to determine the fragmentation fraction. This ratio is calculated relative to a simulated sample that models the $B^0_s$ production in association with charm or beauty quarks. The results are presented for the first time for the case of charm quarks, and for both energy levels in the case of beauty quarks. The results show that, on average, more $b$ quarks fragment into $B^0_s$ mesons compared to $c$ quarks, and this is true for all categories of these particles. The results for $b$ quarks agree with previous measurements at a lower energy of 7 TeV, and for both charm and beauty quarks, the results are in agreement with the EPOS-LHC model.

We are developing a cryogenic platform featuring a 2-T superconducting magnet, and it's intended to support major experiments focused on dark matter and the axion. The experimental setup is being designed with room for future upgrades, and it will have a flexible and adaptable structure. The cryogenic platform's experimental volume is envisioned to be 2.5 meters long, 1.5 meters wide, and 1.0 meter high.

In cryptography, ensuring the security and correctness of cryptographic primitives is vital. Recent studies have found that popular Python crypto libraries are vulnerable to significant security risks due to incorrect usage. This research compares the API designs of Python, Java, and C crypto libraries to uncover differences in how developers are likely to use these tools. We conducted an experiment with a total of 150 participants, split into groups based on their proficiency in cryptography and their primary development language. We created an unrealistic yet representative cryptography use case and asked participants to write code using their respective language's crypto library to complete this task. C groups were further divided based on their declared cryptography knowledge. Our results show a substantial difference between the intended and actual cryptography implementations made by participants. Notably, C participants with declared cryptography knowledge performed significantly better. Our analysis reveals that the API design of Python crypto libraries is significantly more forgiving, while Java and C libraries are much stricter, compelling developers to correctly implement cryptography in the latter languages. This suggests that the API design of Python crypto libraries may encourage more incorrect cryptography implementations.

This paper proposes an advanced 3D reconstruction framework, called 2Big3D, designed to efficiently recover the intricate shapes of massive 3D objects from a single high-resolution 2D image, a task previously thought infeasible. We find that the increased volume of large-scale 2D image data complicates the retrieval of high-quality 3D information. To address this challenge, 2Big3D builds upon the success of established small-scale approaches by first decomposing the massive 2D image into smaller, manageable patches. Each patch is independently processed to generate corresponding 3D details, after which a novel cross-referencing mechanism combines these details to accurately reconstruct the massive 3D object. The efficacy of 2Big3D is demonstrated through a variety of tests, including a comparison with current small-scale approaches on both synthetic and real-world datasets, as well as assessments of its capacity to recover large-scale 2D images into detailed 3D objects.

To solve the inverse problem of seismic data analysis, we propose an innovative reconstruction method for coefficients of subsurface seismic data.  By incorporating sparse synthesis with the total variation model for geometric constraints, we combine it into a single non-convex and non-convex synthesis model that is unique and non-convex.  The proposed model takes advantage of two key characteristics: the sparsity of the coefficients and the geometric constraints, which together improve the recovery of the subsurface reflection coefficients.  Results of our study demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed model in producing more accurate and detailed subsurface images, particularly in comparison to traditional techniques such as L1-norm and Laplace-norm-based methods.  The proposed method outperforms the L1-norm and Laplace-norm-based methods in terms of accuracy, particularly in the case of complex subsurface structures.  Furthermore, we observe that the proposed model is more robust to noise, which allows for improved reconstruction of seismic data.  Overall, we demonstrate the potential of the proposed non-convex and non-convex synthesis model to significantly improve the accuracy of seismic data analysis and interpretation.

The nature of the operator $T_g$, whose $p$-th power is well-defined and acts on $BMOA_p$, a space more expansive than $H^p$, is being examined. We have found that $T_g$, a compact operator from $BMOA_p$ to $p$-convex spaces, is also a finite rank operator for a range of $p$ from 1 to 2. In contrast, a particular function yields an operator from $BMOA_p$ to $q$ that is compact but not of finite rank, under certain conditions.

Our research demonstrates that non-local correlations in low-energy quantum systems can be computed precisely using dynamic real-time analysis. By applying this method to a quantum spin chain, we showed that real-time overlaps between energy levels of different lattice configurations yield a precise tensor product state, the complexity of which scales linearly with system size, thus enabling the calculation of key conformal data points including the central charge, OPE coefficients, and OPE lengths.

A novel application of set-valued prediction is proposed for part-of-speech (POS) tagging, specifically enhancing performance with unknown words. Instead of pre-selecting a fixed number of top POS tags, our approach estimates set-valued probability distributions over all POS tags, which is particularly beneficial during prediction. Experimental results on the English Treebank 3 dataset demonstrate that our approach significantly improves POS tagging performance with novel, unknown words, ultimately leading to an average performance gain of 1.1% on a held-out test set.

This study examines the implications of a sequence of direct utility maximization problems whose demand functions converge in the Euclidean space, specifically whether this convergence in turn implies convergence of the corresponding utility maximization problems' values and optimal demand functions. Our key finding is that under suitable assumptions, a sequence of demand functions converging to a function will result in the limiting function being a demand function, with the convergence occurring in the space of continuous functions. This result is fundamental as it enables the definition of a metric on the set of upper semicontinuous preference relations whose demand sets are nonempty, thus facilitating preference relation convergence in turn.

As urban areas become increasingly intricate, cities are incorporating various technologies to address these complexities, giving rise to the concept of the smart city.
